items.en: The man accused of attacking Helen Haines allegedly made a U-turn before ramming the independent MP twice in an alleged targeted attack near her electorate office, causing her to lose one of her legs.
The member for Indi was airlifted from Wangaratta in northern Victoria to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery on Monday night.
Surgeons were on Tuesday fighting to save Haines’ other leg, as the 65-year-old remained in a critical condition.
The alleged attack on Helen Haines on Monday took place outside her Wangaratta electorate office.

The incident happened about 3.35pm and involved a four-wheel drive, which allegedly U-turned before striking Haines. The independent federal MP is in a critical but stable condition at Melbourne’s Alfred hospital and has lost one of her legs.
A 43-year-old man has been taken to Wangaratta police station for questioning.
The Australian Human Rights Commission has expressed shock and sadness at the attack on Helen Haines. In a post to social media, the commission said:
Everyone should be safe at work and in life. Violence has no place in our society.
Everyone should be treated with respect, irrespective of their political opinions, gender, faith, race or background.

Parliamentarians must be able to carry out their duties safely. This attack happened against a backdrop of increasing polarisation and threats against politicians. We must address intimidation, hatred, threats and violence that undermine our democracy and democratic institutions.
Zoe Daniel: ‘It was obvious … someone would get physically hurt’
The three-time ABC foreign correspondent and former independent member for Goldstein, has written a comment piece after the alleged attack.
It was obvious to those of us who work in and around politics, that eventually, someone would get physically hurt.
The fact that it’s Helen Haines, arguably the best of all of us, not just as a politician but a person, is unbearable.
Some of us community indies have T-shirts that say, “What would Helen do?”
They were a gift from the member for Kooyong, Dr Monique Ryan, a few years ago.
And while it was a bit funny at the time, it’s not a joke.

Helen is the one you go to when you’re grappling with the moral quandaries that arise frequently as an MP, in a job when a binary yes/no vote sometimes feels impossible. With intelligence, warmth and deeply held ethics, she represents the very backbone of the parliament.
‘Don’t send that nasty comment’: Hastie joins calls to turn the temperature down
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie said he’s shocked and saddened by the alleged attack on Helen Haines, and also had concerns about his own safety and of others in Parliament.

“It’s always in the back of my mind”, he said, “which is why I stay fit and I take precautions”. Hastie was recently given extra security by the government due to threats on himself and his family, and says more broadly that the temperature needs to be turned down, particularly on social media.
Speaking to ABC radio this morning, Hastie said:

Be a better steward of Australian democracy. The worst thing we can do right now is point fingers at our political opponents and say, see, it was something that they posted or something that they said. How can we each be better? Maybe don’t like that nasty post or don’t send that nasty comment or don’t trash someone when you don’t even know who they are.

Despite their political differences, he said he held Haines in “very high regard” and called her one of the gentlest and friendliest MPs. It echoed the tributes from other politicians across federal and state parliaments who described her as “the best of us”.
Albanese praises Haines, as MP remains in critical condition
Anthony Albanese is speaking at an event organised by The Age in Melbourne. He says Helen Haines is still in a critical condition in the Alfred Hospital.
Helen Haines represents the best of our political representatives.
Kind, compassionate, a person of integrity, totally committed, strongly representing the people of that beautiful part of Victoria.
I was asked earlier today when someone suggested ‘could we do a vigil somewhere? What can we do to show our support and solidarity between fellows at this difficult time?’
My response to them, when I thought about it, was just ‘be like Helen: kindness, compassion, caring.’
Light will win over darkness: PM reiterates praise for barber who rushed to help
Prime minister Anthony Albanese is speaking in Melbourne and has again praised Rick Jefferies, the local barber who stepped in during the alleged attack against MP Helen Haines.
He says Jefferies’ actions represented the best of the Australian character.
He said it was just the right thing to do, but he did run into danger, not knowing what the consequences could potentially be for him.
Just running to help someone else. A great example of the Australian spirit and the best of the Australian character.
So I think that even in dark times we see light. What Ricky represents is light, and light will be over darkness each and every time.
State and local government representatives across the Indi electorate have released a joint statement condemning the violent attack on Helen Haines.
Our thoughts are with Helen, her family, her staff, and all those affected by this deeply distressing incident.
Helen represents the best of public service. Her commitment to integrity, her respectful engagement in debate, and her sense of democracy and peace are the example we should aspire to.

The statement, signed by Victorian members Tim McCurdy, Bill Tilley, Cindy McLeish and Annabelle Cleeland, along with the mayors of nine local councils said personal threats, intimidation and acts of violence had no place in our democracy. “We will not allow intimidation to silence public voices. Decency still outweighs division, and our communities reject hatred, violence, and fear,” the statement said.
Prime minister meets police commissioners and politicians in Melbourne
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has met AFP commissioner, Krissy Barrett, and her Victorian counterpart, Mike Bush, in Melbourne after the alleged attack on Helen Haines.
The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, and the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, also attended.

If the increasingly vituperative tenor of our public discourse, online and verbal, has fully trailed America’s into the murky dungeon of political violence with the appalling alleged attack on Helen Haines, Australia’s political class has only itself to blame.
Nationals MP says office did not feel threatened by Brendan Nugent
Victorian Nationals MP Tim McCurdy said the alleged attacker, Brendan Nugent, was known to his Wangaratta office and regularly came in to raise different issues.
We get plenty of people come in, half a dozen a day come for various things. So yes, he’s been into our office, [to raise] various issues.
Our office didn’t feel threatened by him. If they had, they would ring the police.
Haines’ alleged attacker has been named as Brendan Nugent
Helen Haines’ alleged attacker has been named as 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, Guardian Australia has confirmed.
Nugent is a long-term forestry campaigner in the state’s north east. Environment campaigners who worked with Nugent several years ago have expressed shock at his arrest.

He has a master’s of forest ecosystems science from the University of Melbourne and spent years researching the forestry industry in Victoria. He has also been a registered business owner in Wangaratta.
Wangaratta locals will unite to pray for the independent MP in a lunchtime vigil at the Holy Trinity Anglican Cathedral.

In a social media post, the Anglican Diocese of Wangaratta says the event is an opportunity for the community to “come together to reflect, have silence, and to pray for Helen, her family and her close friends”.
Our time together is an important act of solidarity with Helen and a sign of peace and goodwill for all people.
Calls for non-violence as Greens leader pays tribute to Helen Haines

The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, has called Helen Haines a “powerful voice for compassion and humanity” and said the notion she could be allegedly targeted for her work is “horrifying, senseless and shameful”.
I believe in politics centred on peace and non-violence because normalising violence in our civil and political debate lowers the threshold for violence.
We cannot let [alleged] political violence become the norm and I believe that politics grounded in non-violence is a powerful way to address this threat.
AFP and Victorian police working to identify potential charges

The Australian federal police commissioner, Krissy Barrett, said in a statement a 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee in Victoria remains in custody and confirmed the event appears to be an “isolated incident”, with no known threats connected to the matter.
Victoria police and the AFP are working to identify potential charges, such as the offence of causing harm to a commonwealth official, which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years’ imprisonment.

Barrett said the AFP had announced the establishment of a “flying squad of hate disrupters” who focus on high-harm, high-impact politically motivated violence, communal violence and hate crimes that do not meet the threshold for terrorism and investigates threats against federal parliamentarians.
The AFP provides regularly briefings to parliamentarians about their safety and security, and further briefings will be undertaken soon.
The AFP’s thoughts are with Dr Haines and her family at this time.

Between 2024 and 2025, the AFP received 951 reports of harassing, nuisance, offensive and threatening behaviour against high office holders, federal parliamentarians, electorate offices and protected establishments. This increased to 1,067 reports the following year.
Jacinta Allan issues first statement since quitting politics on Helen Haines

Former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan has issued her first statement since quitting politics in August, describing Helen Haines as an “outstanding representative for regional Victoria” who has “worked hard every day for her community”.
She said she was “sickened by the [alleged] attack” and that Haines should have been safe doing her job:

Helen was [allegedly] attacked at work, she was doing her job. All members of parliament and their staff deserve to be safe at work. Violence as a substitute for debate must be repudiated at every turn, rejected and condemned unequivocally – by everyone, every time.

The mother of the youngest alleged victim of Alan Jones has told a Sydney court she “trusted” the 2GB broadcaster and was “comfortable” her teenager was going to spend a weekend at his Fitzroy Falls property.

The young man, known as complainant A, has testified that when he was 17 he was alone at the southern highlands farm when Jones allegedly kissed him, put his tongue inside his mouth and touched him on the bottom. “I felt violated and I felt gross,” he told the court earlier.
Complainant A is one of five men who allege Jones, 85, sexually touched them between 2003 and 2020. All five have now completed their evidence as the trial enters its 11th week.
Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching.
A’s mother gave her evidence-in-chief on Tuesday in the Downing Centre local court after her son had spent more than a week in the witness box interrupted by multiple legal arguments.

The divorced mother, who was facing financial ruin and mourning a death in the family, said she “absolutely trusted” Jones as she had read many emails from him in which he said what a wonderful young man her boy was.
“I was just so pleased to have an older mentor in [A’s] life that was interesting and interested in so many things … and saw my son was as intelligent as he is and engaging,” she said.

Jones, who had been corresponding with A since the then 13-year-old asked him for help with his mother’s “dire” financial problems, had never invited her to his home but had invited the teenager on multiple occasions, the court heard.
She said her son had meals with Jones at a local pub and at his Circular Quay apartment but she was never invited.
When her son returned from his two-night stay during the school holidays, the mother said she “knew straight away something was up” because “his mood was different” and he wasn’t sleeping.
“He told me had had broken a plate and he was remorseful about that,” she said. Complainant A earlier told the court Jones was “frustrated, annoyed and angry” when he dropped a $1,500 Versace plate.

Ten days after he returned from Fitzroy Falls her son handed her a “scrawly” note and said “I don’t want to talk about it”, she said as she broke down in tears in the witness box when handed a copy of the note by a court officer.
Her son earlier told the court he wrote a vague account in the note which said he “felt violated at Fitzroy Falls about an incident of a sexual nature”.

She said she read the note and asked her son if he wanted to report the alleged assault to the police. He declined, saying: “I wasn’t raped. It is probably not a big thing in the scheme of it. It will be my word against his and he is a powerful man.”

The witness said she told her son “not to have any contact” with Jones, but she continued to correspond with the broadcaster about issues he had been helping her with, including repairs on her house, which Jones paid for to the tune of $100,000.
Asked why she continued to correspond with Jones, the witness said: “I was scared because I had already asked [A] if he wanted to go to the police” and “nothing with the bank was finalised”.
She said she was afraid Jones could withdraw the assistance he had provided and “that was pretty frightening”.
The witness said she gave her first statement to police several years later, in May 2024.
In December 2025 she found the note and handed it to the detective who was investigating A’s case.

As Republicans confront mounting political headwinds ahead of November’s midterm elections, Donald Trump is attempting to turn unrest in France into a cautionary tale for American voters, recasting the demonstrations that began as student protests against crumbling schools and the soaring cost of living as evidence of the dangers of immigration and the erosion of western civilization.
At a rally in Kansas on Monday evening, Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”.
“If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France,” he said.

Nationwide protests in France on Saturday were called over rising fuel prices and falling purchasing power, and in several cities they erupted into looting and clashes with police that left a historic town hall torched and led to 1,800 arrests. On Monday, overnight curfews were issued for a number of French cities, including parts of Paris.

“This is what’s happening to France – they want to happen to our country. It’s never happening here,” Trump declared, drawing loud cheers from the thousands-strong crowd in ruby-red Kansas where the Republican senator, Roger Marshall, is facing a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton.
Earlier in the day, Trump repeated his baseless claim that migrants had “taken over” France, writing on Truth Social that the country’s leaders must “CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!”

The rhetoric echoes France’s far-right National Rally, whose president, Jordan Bardella, described the violence as a convergence of ultra-left extremism and delinquent populations from the suburbs. Trump and Vance have both publicly backed Marine Le Pen, and the unrest has added pressure on Emmanuel Macron six months before an April election to choose his successor.
As Trump set off for the Kansas rally on Monday, the US president told reporters at the White House that he had warned Macron he was “making a big mistake”.
“The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal,” he said, adding: “We closed our borders. He didn’t.”

Before Trump arrived on stage in Park City, Kansas, giant TV screens played about 10 minutes’ of Fox News coverage of the unrest that has gripped Paris and other cities, which included commentary blaming the trouble on the French government’s immigration policies.

The demonstrations in France began weeks ago, when high school students began marching for teacher shortages, crumbling classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. The CGT, one of France’s largest unions, has backed the movement and called for lower prices, higher pensions and better wages. The anger has since widened to fuel prices, which have climbed since US strikes effectively shut the strait of Hormuz, and other economic grievances.

As the midterms loom, the unrest in France offers Trump a familiar politcal opportunity: the chance to transform a crisis on the other side of the Atlantic into an argument in favor of the hard-line immigration policies that helped propel Trump’s return to the White House.
“If you import the third world, you become the third world,” the official White House X account posted earlier in the day..
JD Vance and array of Republican politicians have lined up to make a similar argument.

Sharing a video that showed the historic city hall in Limoges alight, vice-president JD Vance argued that the rioting was the result of what he called a liberal failure. “Western liberals imported the third world into France,” he wrote on X, adding that the country had “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”.

House Speaker Mike Johnson posted: “France is descending into chaos because they wanted OPEN BORDERS — just like the socialist Democrats in America. What we are witnessing is a chilling warning for all Americans of what happens if the radical Marxist insurgent left gets their way.” Senator Eric Schmitt added: “The anti-civilization Left is devouring France. It will devour America if we let it.”

Not all protests have drawn the same attention from Washington, as young people have taken to the streets across Europe, in Spain, Portugal and Italy, over underfunded schools, housing costs and a wider squeeze on living standards.

Neither has the president commented on protests in Albania, where demonstrators have targeted both the government and a luxury tourism development backed by an investment firm founded by Trump’s close familyson-in-law, Jared Kushner.
But Republicans are eager to keep the attention on France, as they warn of threats to the national identity and seek to rally support for Trump’s Make America Great Again movement.
The vice president said he hoped Americans were paying attention as they cast their ballots.
“This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country,” Vance concluded.

The Trump administration reached a settlement with the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill that will close 18 active federal investigations and a separate Justice Department compliance review involving alleged antisemitism and race discrimination at the university.

The voluntary settlement agreement does not require a monetary payment, and the university does not admit to any wrongdoing or liability. The deal, which will remain effective until the end of 2028, allows UNC to maintain its eligibility for federal funding.

Under the agreement, UNC will appoint an internal "Merit & Civil Rights Administrator" and establish a "Title VI Coordinator" position in its compliance office to address complaints about antisemitism and race-based discrimination.

The university said Elizabeth Hall, associate vice chancellor for university compliance, was appointed to serve in both roles in addition to her existing duties. She will be the point of contact for the Justice Department and oversee UNC's reporting obligations.

"This announcement reinforces our commitment to the fair and equal treatment of everyone at Carolina," UNC Chancellor Lee H. Roberts said in a statement. "For at least a decade, through different presidential administrations, U.S. universities have faced heightened public scrutiny across a range of issues. We’re proud to resolve those issues at Carolina in a way that protects our mission and affirms the civil rights of everyone in our community."
The agreement also requires UNC to provide mandatory antisemitism training to students, faculty and staff.

UNC will also prohibit face masks used to conceal an individual's identity, subject to certain exceptions, as part of the deal, which said student groups "shall be subject to discipline for antisemitic discriminatory conduct."

President Donald Trump and administration officials have accused pro-Palestinian protesters of antisemitism. But protesters, including some Jewish groups, contend that opposing Israel's military offensive in Gaza is not antisemitic and that support for Palestinian rights does not indicate support for extremism.

The settlement agreement also said UNC will adopt what the Justice Department called a "color-blind admissions system," barring the university from using race or altering its admissions process to change the racial composition of its student body. However, it does not prevent UNC from considering how applicants overcame adversity at a personal level, and the university may consider aspects of family background, such as poverty, if those considerations are applied consistently.
UNC must also maintain race-blind policies governing student benefits, scholarships, financial aid and programming, according to the agreement.
The administration has argued that policies favoring certain racial groups over others violate federal anti-discrimination law.
The deal said UNC will send any antisemitism and race discrimination complaints it has received to the DOJ and the Department of Education on a quarterly basis.

As part of the agreement, the Education Department's Office for Civil Rights will close 18 active investigations into UNC, while the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division will close a separate 18-month compliance review opened in April 2025.

"Title VI requires that all students — regardless of their ancestry or race — receive equal treatment under the law at federally funded colleges and universities," Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon said in a statement.

"Higher ed policies and practices that tolerate antisemitism or favor certain racial groups over others, frustrate our color-blind justice system. The Civil Rights Division commends UNC for its cooperation in meeting its obligations under federal law without the need for litigation; we hope other institutions will take note and do the same," she added.
In 2023, the Supreme Court rejected affirmative action at colleges as it struck down race-based admissions programs at UNC and Harvard.

The administration has targeted universities across the country with probes and threats to pull federal funding in response to pro-Palestinian protests on campus, diversity initiatives and transgender policies.

The federal government has also settled with some other schools, including Columbia University, which last year agreed to pay more than $200 million to resolve federal probes, and Brown University, which agreed to provide $50 million over 10 years to Rhode Island workforce-development organizations as part of its settlement.
Harvard, which has been a primary target of the administration's threats, has not yet made a deal.
The Tampa Bay Rays will take on the Milwaukee Brewers, as they defeated the Cleveland Guardians, 7-3, in Game 6 of the ALCS to win the American League pennant.
The Brewers, who shockingly swept the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS, have been watching this ALCS patiently to see who their opponent will be.
Tampa Bay won Game 5 on the road, which is always a pivotal tilt when the series is tied at two games apiece, and they didn’t squander their first trip back home at Tropicana Field.
With a sold-out "Trop," the Rays used their momentum to get the job done.
Richie Palacios got the Rays on the board first in the bottom of the second inning after a clutch, two-out double to make it 2-0 early.
Then, with the game at 3-1 in favor of Tampa Bay, it was their superstar, Junior Caminero, hitting what felt like the series-sealing home run that sent the Trop into rapture.

Caminero turned on an inside pitch and was willing the ball to stay fair, as it smacked off the foul pole and the celebration ensued. Caminero stopped before hitting first base, screaming in elation with the crowd and his nearby teammates in the dugout as he understood making it a 5-1 game in the bottom of the seventh inning was a back-breaker for the Guardians.
Caminero took his time rounding the bases before touching home plate, and the Rays fans in the stadium matched his energy the entire time.

Cleveland, though, wouldn’t go down without a fight. They found some juice in the ensuing frame, scoring twice to make it a 5-3 game. But as they’ve done all season, the Rays responded when they needed it.
Yandy Diaz hit his own home run, and there was no doubt about the 416-footer he sent over the left field wall to give his squad a four-run lead.

As the top of the ninth began, Bryan Baker, the Rays’ lockdown closer, took the mound to finish the job in Game 6. He got Steven Kwan and Jose Ramirez to both ground out to first base before Chase DeLauter popped out foul to punch Tampa Bay’s ticket into the Fall Classic.
This marks the first time the Rays have been to the World Series since the 2020 COVID-19-shortened season, while the Brewers are in for the first time in 44 years.
Either way, one of these franchises will be winning its first-ever World Series as neither have been able to place one in their trophy case in history.

Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers took aim at Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed during a town hall with Fox News host Sean Hannity on Monday, warning voters that his rival's policies would hurt the state.
Rogers accused El-Sayed of having a "pattern of deception" and called him a "manufactured candidate," claiming the Democrat has misrepresented his political positions.
"He is the most extreme candidate. He has called for defunding the police. He has called for letting criminals out of prison," Rogers said.
"He has called for the Green New Deal, which for Michigan is a killer."
Rogers also touted his campaign's ground operation, saying volunteers are approaching 6 million doors knocked across Michigan.
"That's the energy, and what we're getting off of those doors is, 'Yes, we're voting,' 'No, we're not going to be a DSA state,' 'No, we're not going to let this happen on our watch.'"
The Republican also said his campaign is seeing support from voters who traditionally back Democrats.
Rogers later took questions from voters, including a Jewish woman who said she sometimes feels afraid to show her Jewish identity in public.
Rogers said he had heard similar stories from Jewish students at the University of Michigan who said they concealed religious symbols because they were being harassed.
Rogers also pointed to housing, education and skilled trades, saying he wants to make it easier for young adults to buy homes and bring more defense industry work to the state.
He also called for putting shop classes back in Michigan high schools, arguing that expanding skilled-trade education would give students more paths to well-paying careers.
Rogers closed by again targeting El-Sayed's policies, arguing Michigan "cannot afford" them.
"We certainly can't risk his ideology," he said.
El-Sayed's campaign could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment.
Alberta voters decide whether to take a step toward separating from Canada
In Canada, the oil-rich province of Alberta votes in a referendum that could set it on a path toward separation, as Prime Minister Mark Carney warns of threats to Canadian unity.

Voters in Alberta, Canada, are deciding today whether to take the first step toward a referendum on separating from the rest of the country. Reporter Sheena Rossiter joins us from Edmonton, which is the capital of Alberta. Hi there.
SUMMERS: So, Sheena, this vote's a nonbinding referendum. Explain for us a bit more what people in Alberta are voting on today.

ROSSITER: Well, essentially, it's a vote on whether to have another referendum. There are 10 questions covering everything from immigration and provincial services to Alberta's constitutional status. Question 10 is the key one. Voters choose between keeping Alberta in Canada or starting the process towards a separation referendum. If Option 2 wins, it could pave the way for a vote on separation, much like Brexit in the U.K.
SUMMERS: And these separatist sentiments there, how long have they been brewing in Alberta?

ROSSITER: These grievances go back decades. Some people I spoke with at the Alberta independence rally have been separatists for 25 years, like Cory Morgan. He is the founder of Pathway to Independence, a third-party advertising group advocating for an independent Alberta.
CORY MORGAN: Even if we don't get over the line on Monday, I would hope that some people understand something large is brewing here. And if we don't get some change, it's going to continue to grow.

ROSSITER: Separatist sentiment really grew during COVID, with frustration spilling onto the streets during the 2022 trucker convoy in Ottawa. Now, the premier of Alberta, Danielle Smith, called for a referendum but wants Alberta to stay in Canada. And Prime Minister Mark Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, is making the same case, saying, quote, "Canada is stronger together."
SUMMERS: What's really at the heart of this, though?

ROSSITER: Well, Alberta is a major oil-producing province. It's the wealthiest province in the Canadian Confederation, and some residents feel that they contribute more to Canada than they get back. They want to keep more of that money in Alberta. But a government-commissioned report from the University of Calgary estimates that Alberta separating from Canada could cost up to $170 billion Canadian over five years. Thomas Lukaszuk, founder of Forever Canadian, a pro-unity group campaigning against Alberta separation, points to Quebec's 1995 referendum as a warning about the potential economic fallout.
THOMAS LUKASZUK: Several hundred thousand Canadians moved out of the province of Quebec and moved to other provinces. And till today, the province of Quebec hasn't recovered economically from that.
SUMMERS: How soon will we know the results?

ROSSITER: Well, Elections Alberta says unofficial results are expected within 48 hours of polls closing. There's also a legal challenge over Indigenous rights, with the province appealing a court ruling that First Nations weren't properly consulted. And whatever the result, Alberta's place in Canada is likely to remain a major issue heading into next year's provincial election.
SUMMERS: Sheena Rossiter, reporting from Edmonton, Alberta, thanks much.

Solar power is changing agriculture in Pakistan, but some fear it could cause issues
Solar power is transforming agriculture in Pakistan. But in a country already facing water scarcity and extreme weather, some fear their widespread use could cause problems.

Solar power is transforming agriculture in Pakistan. Farmers are using it to run water pumps that lower their electricity costs and boost production. But in a country already facing water scarcity and extreme weather, some fear this will create new problems. Betsy Joles has more.
BETSY JOLES, BYLINE: Muhammad Abdullah (ph) stands alongside a tub full of minnows. It's part of the fish farm he helps run in Sallhoke Chatha, in Pakistan's Punjab province.
MUHAMMAD ABDULLAH: Maripa (ph) silver, bighead grass.

JOLES: He lists off some of the species wriggling in the water below. Once these fish are mature enough, they'll be moved to man-made ponds outside. The water in them needs to be changed frequently. Otherwise, the fish will die. For that, Abdullah uses well water pumped from the ground by a solar-powered motor. The pumps run for around 11 hours a day in the summer, cutting the farm's energy bill by about half.
ABDULLAH: (Non-English language spoken).

JOLES: Only those who have a lot of money can work without solar, Abdullah says. Many in this area got into fish farming because staple crops like wheat and corn didn't grow well there. Thanks to solar, access to groundwater has become much cheaper. But Mudassar Kharal, another fish farmer from the area, says no one is really keeping an eye on how much of it is being used.
MUDASSAR KHARAL: There is no check and balance.

JOLES: Some Pakistani water experts warned that solar-powered pumps could worsen the country's over-extraction of groundwater. Bashir Ahmad, director of the Pakistan Agricultural Research Council, says their use is particularly concerning in areas that are otherwise unfit for farming.
BASHIR AHMAD: Adoption of this saltwater pumping in those areas is really scary.

JOLES: Since 2023, there's been a push to cultivate some unproductive lands under the army-backed Green Pakistan Initiative. It's mostly focused on large-scale corporate farming and promotes the use of solar-powered pumps in arid parts of the country like Balochistan. Proponents believe it will help bring farming up to date with high-efficiency irrigation. Critics say it only adds to water woes. Here's news about a thousand acres of barren land being developed under the project from Pakistani broadcaster ARY.
UNIDENTIFIED REPORTER: Green Pakistan Initiative (non-English language spoken).

JOLES: Pakistan's agriculture industry is supported by a river-fed canal system. But the country's reliance on groundwater has steadily increased in the past few decades as pressure on farmers has grown. Researcher Khalid Jamil wanted to find out whether farmers using solar to power their pumps were extracting more groundwater than those using diesel. His Ph.D. findings, published in the Journal of Agriculture and Food Research last year, found that in 77% of cases surveyed, they were.
KHALID JAMIL: It's just human behavior. If you get something free, you do not feel the need to save it.
JOLES: That means extra stress on the already overburdened aquifer that Pakistan draws from.
JOLES: The paradox is that for individual farmers using solar, water has become one less thing to worry about.
JOLES: In the Punjabi village of Kot Ratta Sakhi, farmer Ibrar Hussain (ph) still relies on diesel-powered pumps to irrigate his rice fields. Solar panels are top of his mind.
IBRAR HUSSAIN: (Non-English language spoken).
JOLES: "Everyone has put them up. We also want to put them up and benefit from them," he says. The question is whether Pakistan can afford any unintended consequences.
For NPR News, I'm Betsy Joles in Punjab Province, Pakistan.

EDMONTON, Alberta — For decades, Alberta separatism remained on the political margins. Now, voters in the oil-rich Canadian province are deciding whether to take the first step toward a future referendum on independence.

The nonbinding referendum vote on Monday is the first time the province has put the question of separation to a public vote, in what Elections Alberta has described as the largest electoral event in the province's history.
Polls indicate that Alberta voters will overwhelmingly reject the option of beginning the legal process toward a referendum on separation.

Pollsters generally estimate that about one in five Albertans support separation from Canada. But the vote has brought the question of Alberta's place in the Canadian federation to the forefront of public debate.
Essentially, this is a referendum about whether to hold another referendum on separation.

There are 10 questions in total. The first nine address immigration, access to provincial services such as health care, education and other social services, and potential changes to the Canadian Constitution. Voters can answer yes or no to each of these questions.

Question 10 offers voters two options. Option 1 asks whether Alberta should remain part of Canada, while option 2 asks whether the province should begin the legal process toward holding a referendum on separation.
Western alienation and grievances against Ottawa date back decades, including to the administrations of Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, Justin Trudeau's father, during the 1970s and 1980s.
"I feel the Canadian system is broken. I know we aren't living in hell on earth. But it's the trajectory we're worried about and where things are going," says Cory Morgan.
Morgan founded the Alberta Independence Party in 2000 and is also the founder of Pathway to Independence, a third-party advertising group that advocates for an independent Alberta.

"Even if we don't get over the line on Monday, I would hope that some people understand that something large is brewing here and if we don't get some change, it's going to continue to grow," Morgan told NPR.

Support for separation intensified among some Albertans following COVID-19 lockdowns and vaccine mandates. Premier Danielle Smith said in May that it was "time to have a vote, understand the will of Albertans on this subject, and move on."
The referendum campaign brought Prime Minister Mark Carney back to his hometown of Edmonton on Friday, where he urged Albertans to keep their province in Canada ahead of the vote.
"A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians," Carney told the rally.

Alberta is one of Canada's wealthiest provinces and is home to the world's fourth-largest known oil reserves. The province contributes to Canada's equalization system, which provides federal funding to provinces with lower fiscal capacity. Some Albertans argue that the province should retain more of its revenue rather than see funds redistributed elsewhere in the country.
"We want to make a new country where we can stop sending our money 1,000 kilometers away in Ottawa," says Jeremy Clive, a 23-year-old pilot and university student from rural Alberta.
Leaving the Canadian federation would not be as simple as holding a referendum.

"It requires negotiating your way out," says Jared Wesley, a political scientist at the University of Alberta. "The Supreme Court has stated clearly that in order to leave, a province must negotiate with nine other provinces and the federal government to secure an amendment to the Constitution to remove themselves."
In 1995, Quebec held a referendum on sovereignty that narrowly rejected independence. The vote helped set the stage for Canada's Clarity Act, which Parliament passed in 2000.

The act states that secession negotiations can begin only after a referendum question and its result meet standards of clarity. It does not specify a fixed percentage that constitutes a clear majority. Any separation would also require constitutional negotiations involving provincial and federal governments.

"It's a bit ironic that separatists are a bit frustrated with the inability to change the constitution and they are using that as a pretext to leave, but, in order to leave, they need to change the same constitution with a much higher threshold for agreement," says Wesley.
What happens if Albertans vote for a separation Referendum?

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has said she will respect the result and begin the process of holding a legally binding referendum, subject to the applicable legal requirements. That would not happen immediately.

The province would also need to consult with First Nations. Treaties between First Nations and the Crown predate Canadian Confederation, and First Nations groups have objected to the idea of an independent Alberta.

In May, an Alberta court ruled that a separatist petition seeking to trigger the referendum violated Indigenous rights because the province had failed to consult First Nations. The province has appealed the decision.
The economic cost of Alberta independence

A government-commissioned report by the University of Calgary's School of Public Policy estimated that separating Alberta from Canada could cost as much as $170 billion Canadian dollars over five years. The report examined two scenarios involving a relatively smooth transition.

Under both scenarios, Alberta's debt would rise substantially as the province assumed a share of Canada's federal debt. The report projected that costs could range from $324 billion to $442.3 billion Canadian dollars.
An independent Alberta would also face billions of dollars in additional interest payments compared with what it currently pays as part of Canada.

Thomas Lukaszak, founder of Forever Canadian, a pro-unity movement, and a former deputy premier of Alberta, has spent 18 months campaigning across the province for Alberta to remain in Canada. He points to Quebec's 1995 referendum as a warning about the potential economic effects of separation.

"Several hundred thousand Canadians moved out of the province of Quebec and moved to other provinces," says Lukaszak. "And until today, the province of Quebec hasn't recovered economically from that because industry and investment has left Montreal and I'm fearing that the same thing would happen to the province of Alberta."
When will the referendum results be available?

According to Elections Alberta, unofficial results for referendums with this many questions will be posted 48 hours after polls close. Recruiting enough staff for the vote has been a challenge, and Elections Alberta staff are expected to work around the clock to tally the results.
"This story won't end once the ballots are counted," says Wesley.
The referendum has highlighted deep divisions among Albertans. The question of separation is likely to remain prominent in the lead-up to the provincial election next year.

The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear a case about the role of race in admissions to selective Maryland middle schools after a group of parents claimed policies discriminated against Asian students in favour of Black and Latino students.

The Supreme Court agreed on Monday to hear the parents’ plea on four academically rigorous “magnet” schools in Montgomery County, a suburb on the outskirts of Washington, DC, in the neighbouring state of Maryland.
The high court said it would weigh whether the parent group has enough evidence of discrimination for the case to move forward.
Lower courts previously dismissed the case because Asian-American students were not underrepresented at the specialised-curriculum schools compared with the pool of students that applied.
If the Supreme Court rules for the parent group, the Association for Education Fairness, it could revive the lawsuit.
The court is expected to hear arguments in the coming months and rule by June.
The Montgomery County school district’s selection process was introduced in the 2021-2022 school year during the COVID-19 pandemic.
It screens all students for academic potential, and then implements a lottery to randomly assign students from that pool to receive enriched instruction at either a magnet school or a local school.

The suit alleged that the screening process makes it harder for Asian-American students, who the challengers said are clustered in “high-performing, low-poverty elementary schools”, to enter the lottery pool.
Part of the process ranks a student’s performance by comparing the student’s test scores against those of other students whose family incomes are at a similar level.

“Under the applicant pool benchmark, the government can set specific racial targets, hit them, and avoid even an inquiry into discriminatory intent,” so long as it has not explicitly called out race in its process, they wrote in their appeal to the Supreme Court.

The case was thrown out in 2022 by US District Judge Paula Xinis. She noted that the percentage of admitted Asian-American students exceeded the percentage of Asian Americans among all applicants to the magnet schools.
Xinis also found no evidence that the lottery policy was implemented with discriminatory intent.
The school system has consistently argued the new admissions policy, called the “Pandemic Plan” due to the timing of its release, is race-neutral.

“The Pandemic Plan is a colorblind lottery,” lawyers wrote in a brief asking the Supreme Court not to take up the case. “Nothing about the Pandemic Plan, its history, or its purpose is offensive to the Constitution.”
Supreme Court justices will now consider whether a group claiming to be targeted by a race-neutral policy must show it was disproportionately harmed to prove intentional discrimination.

The Australian Federal Police (AFP) have said the alleged targeting of independent lawmaker Helen Haines appeared to be an “isolated incident” and there were no known further threats associated with the attack.

Haines was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her office in Wangaratta, about 200km (124 miles) northwest of the state of Victoria’s capital, Melbourne, on Monday, in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called a “deliberate” act.
The 65-year-old underwent surgery overnight, with Australian media outlets reporting on Tuesday that she has lost a leg and remains in critical condition in a Melbourne hospital.
The suspect is in police custody, an AFP statement released on Tuesday said. Local media identified the driver as a 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee, Victoria.

Federal and state police were working “to identify potential charges”, including “the offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years’ imprisonment”, the statement said.
The prime minister said on Tuesday that the vehicle had performed a U-turn before hitting the MP.
“It’s clear that there was a deliberate act here. This wasn’t an accident, someone just skidding off the road,” Albanese told the ABC national broadcaster.
The prime minister said the alleged attacker’s motive remained unknown.
A former nurse, Haines is an independent federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi and is known for her socially conscious policy positions on the environment and transparency.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told ABC Radio that witnesses said Haines was struck twice by the vehicle before a bystander intervened.
Ricky Jefferies ran from his barber shop, restrained the attacker and removed a knife from him after initially believing the incident was a car accident, Australian media reported.
“I heard a loud bang with no brakes. It was crazy; I just ran out to the front to see what’s happening,” Jefferies told reporters outside his shop.
“I didn’t realise the seriousness of the situation initially, and once it became relevant, I just did what I could and what others were already trying to do.”
Foreign Minister Penny Wong said she was shocked by the “deeply disturbing attack” and wished Haines a full recovery in a post on X.

The attack comes after the federal police documented a steady rise in threats and abuse directed towards the nation’s politicians in recent years. Politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security.
Albanese said on Monday that “the temperature has increased in recent times”.
Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action.
She has been praised for her efforts to increase transparency in politics and crack down on corruption.

At a glance, Ray Boe doesn't stand out from the tens of thousands of other foreign workers toiling at countless construction sites that push Bangkok's soaring skyline ever higher.
Unlike most of them, though, the 31-year-old came to Thailand's capital from one of the country's nine camps for refugees who have fled decades of civil strife inMyanmar.
The camps, which hug the Thai-Myanmar border, are home to more than 100,000 people — in some cases since the 1980s, when the refugees first started arriving.
Until a year ago this month, the Thai government had refused to let them leave the camps to find work, forcing most to live hand-to-mouth on foreign donor aid.
That changed in October 2025, after foreign aid cutbacks — mostly by the United States — forced the camps to slash the food support and healthcare they could provide.
Around the same time, fighting between Thailand and Cambodia over territorial claims had sent hundreds of thousands of migrant workers from Cambodia back home, leaving behind a yawning labor gap.
Myanmar refugees allowed to work outside of camps
To cope with the aid cuts and labor deficit, the Thai government reversed decades of policy and began issuing the refugees permits to work outside the camps, to help them meet their own needs.
Ray Boe is one of the 6,800 camp refugees the government said have entered the Thai labor force in the first year of the program.
"After the cuts by USAID and other organizations, there is no more regular support for our daily needs, like rice and other rations. And there is not enough healthcare in the camps anymore," he said.
The cuts forced him and his parents to borrow from neighbors and to pare down their already modest meals.

Since last month, he has earned 400 baht (about $12) a day pouring concrete and erecting scaffolding around what's to be a 12-story apartment building in central Bangkok. He hopes to start sending money home soon.
"It will help us pay for food and other basic needs, and for health are for my parents," Ray Boe said.

"Compared to how we were living in the camp before, it will be a big difference, having my own income and supporting my family on my own, not having to wait for other people to support us day to day," he told DW.
Refugee work program offers hope, but faces a rocky start
The program allows the refugees to work in 43 of Thailand's 76 provinces and in any sector not reserved by law for Thai citizens only.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the government has improved the vocational training on offer inside the camps to better prepare refugees for work outside.

"We are hopeful that this policy would enhance opportunities and empower the [refugees] to realize their potential, as well as contribute to Thai socioeconomic development," said Praporn Waenluang, a spokesman for the ministry's information department.
Labor and refugee rights groups have welcomed the program.

"I have met a lot of camp [refugees] who have come outside and worked. They are so happy to work and earn money, a lot of money compared to what they [can] get in the camp," said Siwawong Sooktawee, Thailand project coordinator for the International Detention Coalition.
"This is good because they feel they can help themselves, they can support themselves, not depend on aid anymore," he added.
Yet he and others have said the program has gotten off to a slow start, with many flaws to work out.

They said many of the refugees who have taken part have not been given contracts by their employers, only to find the conditions rougher, the work harder, or the pay lower than what they were promised before leaving the camps. The program also lacks a clear system for lodging and settling complaints, according to observers.

"Many refugees go, come back, go, come back so many times. Some refugees, their families have to raise funds or borrow money in the refugee camps so that their father or their family member will be able to return," said K'nyaw Paw, general secretary of the Karen Women's Organization, an NGO serving the camp's ethnic Karen group.
Financial burdens placed on Myanmar refugees

Siwawong and K'nyaw Paw said refugees are sometimes made to repay employers through wage deductions for hiring them, including medical exams, government permits and transportation to job sites. As a result, they often start work already in debt, sometimes without prior warning.

Akwah, a father of two who goes by one name, left his camp with 20 other refugees in November 2025 for what was supposed to be a job harvesting sugarcane on a farm on the other side of the country for 250 baht per day.

When he arrived, however, he was told to cut eucalyptus trees — a much more difficult and dangerous job, he said — for only 200 baht per day. Workers had to sleep outdoors, with no electricity and only a nearby pond for water.
"We spoke to the boss, but the boss did not care. He said, 'Just do the work because you are already here.' But we said we could not do it," said Akwah. They left after three months.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not reply to DW's request for comment on the program's alleged problems. The Labor and Interior ministries, which mainly oversee the program, did not reply to requests for an interview either.
Rights groups say program still needs to improve

Siwawong and K'nyaw Paw said refugees who take part should be guaranteed clear and detailed contracts — translated if needed into Burmese, Karen or Karenni, the main languages spoken in the camps — and an easy-to-access system for filing and settling complaints.
They also suggest that the government open more provinces up to the program and screen the job brokers coming to the camps as middlemen, to weed out the unscrupulous ones.

They said their NGOs and others are working with the government on making some of the upgrades, and that they're hopeful the program will improve with time, so that more of the refugees are able and willing to take part.
For all the program's flaws, though, they said most of the refugees are still eager to apply, even those who have run into problems.

"I had a bad experience, but I still want to go again, because food in the camp is a problem," said Mu Dah Hsit, who fell ill at her job and had to quit after her boss refused to cover the health insurance the program is supposed to guarantee.
"I have no mother, and a father who is sick, and siblings I have to take care of," she said. "So, I have to go; otherwise, we cannot live."

For ten years, publishers rejected You Yeong-Gwang's book. Yet before it was even printed in South Korea, the once-abandoned manuscript had international publishers flocking to secure translation rights.

"I'm so grateful that the book has now been published in more than 20 countries. Even more astonishingly, it also appeared on the Der Spiegel bestseller list in Germany," he told DW while attending the 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair.
For a debut novel by an unknown author, it was a massive success, securing publication in 15 languages, including English, German, Spanish and traditional Chinese.

"The Rainfall Market" tells the story of a mysterious, hidden shop that only opens when it rains. In the shop, visitors can exchange their deepest unhappiness for a ticket to a brand-new destiny. The plot revolves around Serin, a disheartened young girl who stumbles into the marketplace run by whimsical spirits, finding a warm, comforting space.
"In fact, Serin's story is my story," author You said. "For a long time, I even wondered how wonderful it would be if I could sell my unhappiness and use the money to buy happiness."
While writing the book, he was going through a difficult time himself.
"I had to care for my mother, who had been ill for a long time, and I had also been responsible for supporting my family financially for many years. Life felt incredibly heavy," he reflected.

"But when I was writing, I could immerse myself in the world of the story and, even if only for a short while, forget about those circumstances. That's why writing made me so happy. I truly enjoyed it."
On the creation of 'The Rainfall Market'
The idea of rain is inspired by his own life.
"At that time, my circumstances felt as though it were raining constantly," You said.
The story draws heavily on traditional Korean folklore, serving as a quintessential "healing fiction" tale in which its young protagonist must weigh the true cost of seemingly perfect lives.
"When I was writing, I wasn't consciously trying to write healing fiction. At the time, I didn't even really know that such a label existed."

He initially planned to publish a book independently and started crowdfunding. But as the funding failed, he used all his savings and printed 200 copies, which bookstores refused to take. In a month, he only sold five copies. "I thought that's it. I really have to give up now.”

"At the time, I had undergone eye surgery and due to complications, I couldn't see, so I started working at a call center, where I could work using my voice." You said. "During the week, I worked at a call center, and on weekends I went to a computer academy. I learned how to make books on my own for a few years."
He then taught himself how to use the software needed to create books on his own.

While running one of the crowdfunding campaigns, he started working as a food delivery driver. "The round trip between my home and the area where I delivered food took about four hours each day. So I wrote on my phone's memo app while traveling on the subway."

"Even when I was going through very difficult circumstances, I was able to keep writing because the moments when I was writing were so joyful. For a little while, I could forget about the difficult situation I was in," You explained.
"I gathered those pieces of writing together and launched what I intended to be my final crowdfunding campaign," he said.
The campaign was intended to fund the publication of "The Rainfall Market."
"To my amazement, the campaign succeeded, and I was able to publish the book commercially for the first time," he said.
Following the crowdfunding success, the novel was acquired by Clayhouse, a prominent South Korean publishing company.
Before it was even published, he had received offers from publishers in five countries and signed international publishing contracts.
And in the first month after publication, the original South Korean language edition sold 30,000 copies across all formats, ranking as the bestselling e-book and third-bestselling physical book.
"I still find it hard to believe that all of this has happened and that I'm here at the Frankfurt Book Fair. I'm incredibly grateful and happy," said You.
A new horizon for Hallyu, or the 'Korean Wave:' K-Comfort Fiction
Korea's newest soft power is K-literature, which sold about 1.2 million translated copies abroad in 2025 for the second consecutive year.
And You's book belongs to a trending genre called Korean comfort fiction.
"When readers closed the book, I wanted them to feel a little warmth in their hearts," he said.

Although Korean literature was first known for darker, more pragmatic books about societal realities, K-comfort fiction is the child of South Korea's pressure-cooker modern society. It offers an answer to the human need for escapism and a transient antidote to the reality of a hyper-competitive education system, brutal job market and intense corporate pressure.

"When I was writing, I was going through a very difficult time myself, and I wished someone would comfort me. So, I thought, why don't I try reading something like that myself? Why don't I write something that can comfort me?" You wondered.

With burnout on the rise globally, more readers are seeking soul-soothing literature with exhausted protagonists they can relate to. Usually without a need to defeat a villain, the stories follow protagonists with a deep desire for rest, community and emotional repair.

The whimsical fiction aspect is the missing element allowing them to step away from reality. The genre originally gained traction through indie productions, online crowdfunding and endorsements from high-profile K-pop artists.

Despite the Korean context, this style of storytelling quickly went global, capturing different international audiences, including those already familiar with cozy K-dramas or those simply looking for a gentle refuge from the anxieties of the modern world.

Last year, the bestselling Korean novel abroad was "Welcome to the Hyunam-dong Bookshop," according to the Literature Translation Institute of Korea. The novel belongs to the same genre as "The Rainfall Market."

While readers embrace the genre, critics view it with literary skepticism. They point out that it relies heavily on a predictable, repetitive formula, often built around a single magical space, with simplistic prose and low-stakes conflicts that prioritize cozy vibes over deep character development.

Reviewing "The Rainfall Market" for the Korea Times, Peter Juhl, a literary critic, described healing fiction as light, feel-good stories and argued the boom reflects a deliberate effort to write global novels for international markets.
Future aspirations and message to readers

"Of course I'm happy that my book is receiving so much love and that I'm able to write. But more than anything, I hope my mother gets better and regains her health," You said after mentioning that his mother underwent surgery a week before his arrival at the book fair.
Beyond the book itself, people seem to relate to and appreciate the story of his own life.

"If I have the opportunity, I'd like to share more stories about hope and dreams with people who are going through circumstances similar to mine," said You. "If my story can help one person even a little, in any way, I don't think anything could make me happier."
4 soldiers from El Salvador missing in Haiti after attack by gangs
Soldiers believed to have fled burning vehicle, but are since accounted for

Gangs in Haiti opened fire on an armoured vehicle over the weekend, leaving four soldiers from El Salvador unaccounted for in the first major attack since an international gang suppression force began operations in the violence-wracked Caribbean country.
The attack occurred Sunday in Croix-des-Bouquets, a once-peaceful community in Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince, that is now controlled by violent gangs.
The armed forces of El Salvador said in a statement Monday that the four aviation technicians were returning to camp when their armoured vehicle was attacked with explosives and set on fire.
The military noted that the four men managed to flee the burning vehicle and it is working with international forces to "establish contact and determine the location of our military personnel."
Salvadoran authorities said that helicopters were dispatched to the area but they, too, came under fire as they dispersed armed men in the area.

"Multiple attempts to approach by land and air have been made, but these have been hampered by the intensity of the fighting," the Salvadoran military said.

"This latest episode is a reminder, as if we really needed one, of the fact that the security challenges in Haiti are complex and complicated," he said.

"To the gangs and gang leaders who carried out this cowardly attack, if you think you're going to intimidate this coalition into retreat, you have made a terrible mistake," he said.

He warned that gangs have carried out reprisal killings in some areas following operations by Haitian and international forces, and that they have pushed deeper into places including the community of Kenscoff and the Artibonite region.
"The reality is that we cannot be everywhere at once," Christofides said.
The area where the armoured vehicle was targeted is controlled by gangs including Chèn Méchan, Kraze Barye and 400 Mawozo.

No one has claimed responsibility for the attack on the Salvadoran troops. It comes as Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade and showcases the power of the gangs that control an estimated 70 per cent of Port-au-Prince.

For the last month, the weather radars across south-eastern Australia have been lighting up with precipitation every night.
The only problem is that on most nights, skies are not cloudy and it certainly has not been raining for a month straight.
"There has been increased 'echoes' displaying on radars across eastern New South Wales that aren't precipitation," a spokesperson for the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) said.
But the equipment is not malfunctioning, and this is not a giant UFO.
Instead, the radars are detecting the millions of bogong moths currently migrating south to the Australian Alps for summer, and the swarm appears on radar as widespread rain.
The false echoes are appearing like clockwork just after sunset as the moths take flight after spending daylight hours resting and hiding.
Initially, most of the radar anomalies were concentrated in NSW, but recent nights have also seen the phenomenon across northern and eastern Victoria.
Below is the Monday night radar loop, which shows the odd shower and thunderstorms in the late afternoon. However, the arrival of nightfall coincides with a sudden burst of activity.
Why are weather radars mistaking moths for rain?
A radar works by sending out a short pulse of radio waves, then waiting for the signal to bounce back off airborne particles.

If no echoes are returned, the radar imagery will stay blank. But if the waves reflect off raindrops, hail, or snowflakes, the radar can construct a 3D picture of the precipitation pattern based on the height of the beam, along with both the intensity and the return time of the pulses.
However, there are far more objects floating around in the sky than just precipitation.
Bushfire smoke, aircraft, flocks of birds, and swarms of insects can also result in a return signal, as can mountain ranges and tall buildings.
And the atmosphere itself can lead to deception. Certain conditions can cause the radar beam to bend downwards, a process called ducting, and strike the ground.
Exactly how much of the current interference is from moths is unknown. However, there are a number of clues which suggest a large proportion is currently from the millions of bogongs:
- The false echoes are appearing at around the same time every night which matches the diurnal behaviour of the moths
- The coverage of the radar echoes matches the sightings of moths
- The pattern is widespread light rain, which resembles insects more than ducting
What weather watchers are seeing each night is confirmed by the BOM
"Large numbers of insects can look like very light widespread rain, particularly near sunrise and sunset," the spokesperson said.

While meteorologists are not normally fooled by radar interference or clutter, some weather apps that give alerts for imminent precipitation could be sending false alarms, since their algorithms may rely on raw radar data that has not been quality-checked or verified.
However, during the 2000 Olympics, bogong moths did give forecasters a quick flutter.
A crack team of BOM meteorologists predicted a clear and dry night for the closing ceremony, but as the event began, the radar indicated rain was about to hit the stadium.
The meteorologists were puzzled, and their panic only abated when the live broadcast showed a large moth landing on Yvonne Kenny as she performed the Olympic anthem
In this case, a swarm of moths had been attracted to the bright lights of the stadium.
The prolonged spell of interference this year has made radar interpretation less reliable. However, on nights when it is actually wet, it takes a keen eye to differentiate real rain from the clutter.
Take the image below, captured over central-eastern NSW on October 2.
A band of rain is approaching Sydney from the west, while a clump of false echoes is present from northern Sydney to the Lower Hunter.
Thankfully, standard weather forecasts are not affected, since they rely on weather modelling, ground observations and satellites.

Haiti: Elections on hold as gangs adapt to security crackdown, Security Council hears

Armed groups in Haiti are adapting to intensified security operations, stepping up reprisals against civilians and extending their reach into rural areas, the UN warned the Security Council on Monday.

The briefing came two weeks after presidential and legislative elections planned for 13 December were postponed indefinitely, with the UN’s top official in the country cautioning against setting new dates without a realistic assessment of whether a vote can be held.
- 1,123 Haitians were killed and 440 injured in gang-related violence between July and early October
- Sexual violence remains widespread, with 689 women and girls reportedly raped by gang members in July and August
- The Security Council-authorised Gang Suppression Force is not yet fully deployed

In Haiti, security forces are intensifying their operations, but the gangs are not giving up. They are adapting their tactics, increasing reprisals against civilians and spreading violence to rural areas, according to the Secretary-General’s latest report.
“What is particularly worrying is the gangs’ ability to adapt their tactics as security operations intensify,” said Carlos Ruiz Massieu, the UN’s top official in Haiti.
Armed groups are increasingly resorting to hostage-taking, intimidation and reprisals against civilians to maintain their territory and challenge state authority.
The attack carried out on 23 and 24 August in Kenscoff, a mountainous town southeast of the capital, Port-au-Prince, illustrates this strategy.
At least 47 people were killed, 22 wounded, and 52 taken hostage, 13 of whom were later freed thanks to local initiatives supported by the UN.
In the West and Artibonite departments, 241 people were killed for allegedly resisting gangs.
Other attacks – notably in Saint-Michel-de-l’Atalaye, Marigot, and Léogâne – indicate a spread of violence into rural areas. Armed groups are also targeting farmland, homes and public infrastructure.

Security force operations also contribute to the rising death toll. They account for 52 per cent of Haitians killed or wounded since the beginning of July, or 808 people, including 148 not associated with gangs.
Faced with this violence, the Security Council-backed Gang Suppression Force, logistically supported by the UN, is continuing its deployment.
As of 12 October, it had 1,563 uniformed members, far fewer than the 5,550 authorised by the Security Council. It has notably established a base in the Artibonite region, beyond the capital.
But, armed groups retain the capacity to retaliate.

On Sunday, an armoured vehicle transporting Salvadoran soldiers from the force was attacked in Croix-des-Bouquets, in the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area. Four soldiers were still missing on Monday, according to media reports.
For Mr. Ruiz Massieu, retaking territory will not be enough.

“Experience has shown that security operations alone cannot bring about lasting stabilisation,” he warned, calling for the permanent restoration of the State’s presence and the development of disarmament and reintegration programmes, particularly for children recruited by gangs.
This persistent insecurity also jeopardises the return to democracy, he said.
Presidential and legislative elections, initially scheduled for 13 December, have been postponed indefinitely. Haiti has not held national elections since 2016.

Nevertheless, preparations are ongoing. More than 35 political parties and groups, and 3,500 candidates have registered, according to Mr. Ruiz Massieu. As of 5 October, however, only 759,257 potential voters were on the lists, out of an estimated electorate of 6.5 million people. Insecurity and mass displacement are further complicating the organization of the election.
“Setting new dates for elections without a realistic assessment of their feasibility will only erode public confidence and the credibility of Haitian institutions,” he warned.
Adding to this political uncertainty is a humanitarian crisis.
Nearly 1.5 million people have fled their homes, including more than 740,000 children.
The economy is expected to contract for the seventh consecutive year, while the UN’s 2026 humanitarian plan is only about half funded.
The country thus remains faced with a dual emergency: restoring security essential for holding elections, without which a return to democratic institutions remains out of reach.

Millennials get a lot of flak for being overly nostalgic, but I don't think that's fair. When the modern-day world has nothing to offer us but AI slop, shrinkflation and a sad acceptance that we can't be bothered to do anything about global warming. It's easy to see why we yearn for the days of Pogs, the Backstreet Boys, and Saved by the Bell.

One area that we definitely had it good in the 90s was sci-fi, when legendary shows like Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stargate SG-1, and — of course — The X-Files ruled our TV screens long before the age of streaming services. You can relive those glory days of alien conspiracies, spooky happenings and cell phones the size of a brick with the Lego Ideas The X-Files set.

This 1478 piece set is essentially two dioramas crammed into a single display piece. The top of the model depicts a spinning UFO floating above one of those iconic coniferous forests that dominated 90s sci-fi. Why? Because — thanks to some generous tax credits — it was cheaper to shoot in Vancouver, so that's where they all flocked.
Catch Mulder and Scully in every season of The X-Files on Hulu, which is available bundled with Disney+ for only $11.99/month for the first six months, then increasing to $12.99/month.

Beneath the woodland scene, though, is the real star of the show: Mulder's office, squirrelled away in the basement of the FBI's J. Edgar Hoover Building in Washington, D.C. This dingy little office is where Scully meets "Spooky Mulder", kicking off a glorious sci-fi odyssey that would last for eleven seasons (and two movies).

Mulder's dingy little base of operations has been stunningly recreated here, with both overt references and subtle nods that X-Files fans will appreciate. The iconic "I want to believe" poster adorns the wall, alongside photographs of crop circles and a newspaper clipping from a paper called "The Lone Brickman" — a nice nod to "The Lone Gunmen". There's even an actual X-File sitting on the desk, and a cute Lego spoof of the "Face on Mars", with a photo on the wall that shows a Lego head on the moon.

It's been a hot minute since I watched The X-Files (that DVD box set beside my TV is calling to me), but even so, I had a blast building my way down memory lane, remembering episodes as I assembled the diorama. I love the little touches, like the display cabinets filled with artifacts, the VHS tapes scattered around the office and the black oil spillage on the floor.

As with most Lego sets, the minifigures are half the joy. You get Mulder and Scully, obviously, with the dynamic duo of FBI agents both rocking flashlights (no smartphones with built-in lights back in the 90s). Mulder is wearing dark blue, while Scully is rocking an orangey brown suit, with both of them sporting an FBI badge.

Outside of the principal pair, you also get Skinner, Mr X, and the Cigarette Smoking Man. Mulder's partner-turned-nemesis Alex Krycek also gets a suitably devious-looking minifig. It's the gloves, they just make him look like a bad man (which, to be fair, he is). Finally, to ramp up the paranormal scale, we also get a pair of monster minifigs: a grey alien and Flukeman minifigures. The grey alien was a must-have, especially given the UFO floating atop this display piece, but the one-off monster of the week, Flukeman, felt like a weird choice.
Also, this John Doggett erasure will not stand. Sure, he could never replace Mulder, but Robert Patrick's seasons eight and nine run was excellent and he deserved a spot here.

And while I'm voicing minor gripes, the usual Lego FOMO tricks were in force with this set; if you pre-ordered, you got an exclusive gift set — Scully's Lab — free of charge. This extra little diorama isn't necessary, but it does feel like the collection is incomplete without it and it's not for sale separately, so you'll have to try your luck with eBay scalpers if you want it.

Speaking of Scully, Gillian Anderson has stated that after season 11 wrapped in 2018, she was done with the role. That wasn't entirely accurate, though, as she donned the lab gloves one more time for the Lego X-Files set advert. It's a short bit of fan service, but a nice touch, and, once again, it sparks those 90s neurons.

All these delicious Member Berries come at a price, though, and that's the price. This blast from the past will set you back $199 (£179 in the UK). That's no small chunk of change. But then again, anyone who wants this set is in their thirties or forties and can probably afford that outlay for the nostalgia trip. And look at it this way: when The X-Files debuted back in 1993, the price would only have been about $86.

I had a great time building the Lego X-Files set and if you're a fan of the series, you will too. Nostalgia often feels like a cheat code to our hearts, but there's nothing wrong with that. We deserve to remember the good times and the truth is that The X-Files was about as good as it ever got for sci-fi fans.
You can buy the Lego X-Files set now, available for $199/£179 from the Lego store.
