Japan's groundbreaking mission to Mars is officially underway, headed to the Red Planet's mysterious moons Phobos and Deimos for a historic sample-return attempt.

The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission launched today (Oct. 19) from Tanegashima Space Center in Japan, riding an H3 rocket that lifted off from Pad-2 at Tanegashima's Yoshinobu Launch Complex at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. local time in Japan on Oct. 20).

The JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency)-led MMX mission is bound for Mars orbit, where it will study the planet's two moons, Phobos and Deimos. If everything goes according to plan, MMX will become the first spacecraft to land on and return samples from Phobos for study back on Earth, which scientists think could shed light on a decades-old mystery about the moons' origins and reveal clues about the formation of the early solar system.

It was the 10th liftoff of Japan's expendable, two-stage H3 rocket, which was jointly developed by JAXA and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. After clearing its launch pad today, the 207-foot-tall (63 meters) launch vehicle flew a nominal trajectory through its ascent corridor over the Pacific Ocean, jettisoning its four solid boosters in pairs just before the flight clock reached two minutes. The rocket shed its payload fairings about one minute and 20 seconds later, exposing MMX to the vacuum of space for the first time.

H3's first stage, powered by two LE-9 rocket engines, channels a mixture of liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen to produce a combined thrust of 331,000 pounds (1,471 kN), according to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. As the mission clock approached T+5 minutes, H3 executed its main engine cutoff procedure and separated from the second stage, which ignited its engines for a 5.5-minute burn about 10 seconds later.

All continued to go to plan after that. The H3's upper stage ignited its engine for a second time for a trans-Mars injection burn about one hour and four minutes after liftoff, a maneuver that lasted roughly six minutes and 25 seconds and took MMX to a maximum velocity of about 24,145 mph (38,858 kph).

MMX was released from the rocket's upper stage right on schedule, about one minute after the completion of that burn and roughly 71 minutes after liftoff. The success elicited loud cheers in mission control, which viewers saw and heard on JAXA's launch webcast.

MMX is now under its own power, and on course for Mars. The interplanetary transit will last about 10 months, with the spacecraft scheduled to arrive at the Red Planet in August 2027. When it does, MMX's propulsion module will execute an orbital insertion burn to place itself in a quasi-satellite orbit (QSO) around Phobos, which places MMX within the space around the moon as both circle Mars.

MMX will spend about three years in the Martian system, devoting much of that time to studying the 14-mile-wide (22 km) Phobos with its science instruments. The spacecraft also carries the IDEFIX rover, a joint effort of the space agencies of France and Germany, which is scheduled to deploy to the surface of Phobos in late 2028 or early 2029.

After a mapping campaign to select suitable landing sites, MMX will perform two separate touchdowns on Phobos to collect and stow samples in the spacecraft's return capsule. Following its second landing and sample collection, MMX will briefly return to QSO with Phobos before transferring to a more elongated orbit around Mars that intersects with the planet's smaller moon, Deimos, which is just 8 miles (14 km) in diameter.

During the last several months of its time around Mars, MMX will perform a series of Deimos flybys before departing for Earth in November 2030. If all goes according to plan, the MMX sample-return capsule will land in Australia in 2031.

Scientists are counting on those samples, and other data collected during MMX's time around Mars, to answer a decades-old question surrounding the Martian moons' origins. Competing theories and conflicting evidence point to two possibilities for how Mars got its moons.

Their near-circular, equatorial orbits suggest a narrative similar to how Earth's moon is thought to have formed — as a result of a massive planetary impact between Mars and some other giant space rock, which broke off pieces of the planet that eventually coalesced to form the natural satellites that orbit there today.

Neither Phobos nor Deimos is spherical, isntead; both are oblong and lumpy, like potatoes. That fact — along with their chemical composition, as far as we have been able to tell using telescopic spectroscopy — point to the possibility that Phobos and Deimos were asteroids from the early solar system that were captured by Mars' gravitational pull. Figuring out the moons' true origin story would provide key clues about Mars' geological past, the solar system's early history and the formation of the inner planets, mission team members have said.

Once the MMX samples are safely returned to Earth, scientists will study their composition and mineralogy, then compare such chemical fingerprints with those of Martian rocks and asteroid material. These analyses, combined with data collected by MMX during its mission, will help nail down the origin of Phobos — and by extension, Deimos. — by

While JAXA leads MMX, the mission is an international effort, with interagency partnerships between JAXA, NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA), as well as U.S. and European companies, which supplied a handful of the spacecraft's scientific hardware and communications equipment.

NASA's contributions to MMX include the Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons (MEGANE, pronounced "meh-gah-nay") device, which is a gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer built by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL); a Honeybee Robotics-built pneumatic sampler; and communications support using the agency's Deep Space Network.

NASA has also invested approximately $87 million through the end of the mission, which includes funding for United States scientists and astromaterials experts on the MMX team. The agency is getting something concrete for such contributions: At least 15% of the planned 10-gram (0.35 ounces) returned Phobos sample will be reserved for NASA's study. Those materials will be transferred and maintained at the agency's Johnson Space Center in Houston for analysis and long-term preservation.

MMX is not the first Phobos sample-return project to take flight, by the way. That distinction goes to Russia's Phobos-Grunt ("Phobos-Soil") mission, which launched in November 2011 but failed to get out of Earth orbit due to a rocket glitch. The 14.5-ton spacecraft eventually crashed back to Earth over the Pacific Ocean in January 2012.

Just 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer's, scientists find

- Walking just 3,000 steps a day could help slow Alzheimerâs-related brain changes, according to new research. Scientists discovered that physical activity was linked to less buildup of harmful tau proteins and nearly half the cognitive and functional decline, even in people already showing early signs of the disease. The strongest benefits appeared at 5,000 to 7,500 daily steps, suggesting that the popular 10,000-step goal may not be necessary.
A new study suggests that even low levels of physical activity could protect the brain from Alzheimer’s disease – but not in the way scientists expected.

The researchers tracked almost 300 older adults with early brain signs of Alzheimer’s for nine to 11 years using pedometers. They found that physical activity didn’t reduce the toxic amyloid plaques that most Alzheimer’s treatments now target.

Instead, in people who already had these plaques, physical activity reduced the accumulation of misfolded tau proteins in specific brain areas. These proteins appear later in Alzheimer’s disease and are more closely linked to cognitive and functional decline. These signs of dementia were reduced by almost half in more active participants.

Benefits appeared at just 3,000 steps – roughly half an hour of walking at a moderate pace. The optimal range was 5,000 to 7,500 steps daily, after which the effect plateaued. More steps didn’t necessarily mean greater protection, which suggests a realistic target for older, sedentary people, rather than the often-cited 10,000 steps.

The study had limitations, however. It involved a fairly small group of mostly white, well-educated people in the US, and it didn’t take other lifestyle or health factors into account. Also, there may be other protective mechanisms of walking at play. But it does support other research suggesting that being physically active may lower the risk of dementia.

A UK study of 1,139 people over 50 found that those who were moderately to vigorously active had a 34-50% reduction in dementia risk when followed over eight to ten years. Among those who developed dementia, staying active reduced their memory decline, particularly in older women.
A larger 2022 UK study tracked 78,430 people for seven years using wrist accelerometers. It found a 25% reduction in dementia risk with just 3,800 steps daily, rising to 50% at 9,800 steps.

However, people who walked more also had better cardiovascular health – lower cholesterol, better sleep and blood pressure and reduced diabetes risk. Since these heart and stroke risk factors also increase dementia risk, the picture is complex.

Healthy habits often go together. People who exercise are more likely to eat well, not smoke, look after their heart health and have fewer financial stresses. This makes it hard to know which factor is having the biggest effect. The researchers tried to account for this, but because these habits are so closely linked, it’s difficult to say that exercise alone is responsible.

However, there is a strong case for this as there are multiple ways exercise might support the brain: improving cardiovascular health, increasing blood flow and boosting chemicals that promote brain-cell connections.

One such substance is irisin, a hormone produced by muscles that acts on almost all faulty brain mechanisms associated with Alzheimer’s, including inflammation. This and other chemicals, such as BDNF, associated with exercise, provide plausible biological pathways for how physical activity might directly influence brain health beyond its cardiovascular benefits.

But the relationship might work in reverse, too. People may become less active because of early Alzheimer’s symptoms. Those with hearing problems, for instance – itself a dementia risk factor – often report barriers that make them stop being active before other dementia symptoms appear.

Reduced activity then accelerates memory decline. This creates a vicious circle. Early disease symptoms – such as not hearing – can affect self-esteem and reduce engagement in physical activity, which in turn worsens cognitive decline.

Brisk walking might be particularly beneficial. A small trial of 15 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer’s who did Nordic walking (an enhanced walking technique that uses poles to work your upper body as well as your legs) maintained brain function over 24 weeks, with some functions even improving.

The 15 who received only standard care showed decline or no improvement. Though small, the trial suggests that even people already diagnosed with Alzheimer’s might benefit from increased physical activity, including brisk walking.

Getting outside, particularly in nature, may be especially beneficial for preventing dementia – possibly because it improves mood and sleep while reducing isolation – all dementia risk factors. The combination of physical movement, natural light exposure and social interaction when walking outdoors may create multiple protective effects that complement each other.

The challenge now is helping people overcome barriers to outdoor activity, such as safety concerns, fear of falling, or simply preferring the comfort of the sofa – particularly during wetter, colder months. But the evidence suggests that even a few minutes of walking could make a difference, and that modest, achievable targets – a half-hour stroll rather than a marathon training regime – may offer substantial protection against cognitive decline.

A simple touch can bring dying corals back to life in just 7 weeks
Scientists discovered that dying corals can recover in record time simply by touching healthy clones, opening a promising new path to saving threatened reefs.
- Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability

- Scientists have discovered that severely bleached corals can make a remarkable comeback simply by touching healthy, genetically identical corals. In laboratory experiments, dying corals regained their color and fully recovered within seven weeks, with as little as five days of contact sometimes enough to start the healing process.
For the first time, researchers have demonstrated that severely bleached corals can fully recover after spending just a few days in contact with healthy, genetically identical corals.

In laboratory experiments, corals that had turned white and were close to dying regained their health within seven weeks. According to a study published on October 14 in Science Advances, this represents the fastest documented recovery from coral bleaching. The discovery could lead to new techniques for restoring coral reefs, which some estimates suggest could disappear within decades as climate change fuels increasingly severe and frequent marine heat waves.

Coral bleaching occurs when rising ocean temperatures cause corals to lose the beneficial algae living inside their tissues. These algae supply much of the energy corals depend on for growth and survival. Without them, corals lose their vibrant colors, struggle to obtain enough nourishment, and become more susceptible to harmful algae. Even when they survive, regaining their health can take months or years.

"While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet," said lead author Danny Collins, an oceans PhD student at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability. "The question we wanted to answer is, once a coral has bleached, what can we do?"
An Unexpected Discovery Reveals a Way to Rescue Dying Corals

Although they may resemble plants or rocks, corals are animals. In most coral species, individual animals reproduce by creating genetically identical copies of themselves. These clones grow together into large colonies that form the foundation of coral reefs.

The idea for the study emerged from an unexpected observation in 2025. Steve Palumbi, a study coauthor and the Jane and Marshall Steel, Jr. Professor in Marine Sciences, noticed something unusual in his laboratory. Two fragments taken from the same coral colony, one healthy and the other bleached, had fallen against each other in an aquarium.
Where the fragments touched, the bleached coral began regaining its color. The change suggested that beneficial algae were returning to its tissues.

At roughly the same time, Collins was investigating how coral diseases develop and spread. He was particularly interested in bacteria carried by plastic debris that lands on corals and can introduce harmful microorganisms through direct contact.

"Harmful bacteria enter corals through physical contact," said Collins, who is also a Knight-Hennessy Scholar. "We were curious about what would happen if we used contact to reintroduce something good - the beneficial algae from healthy corals."
To investigate, Collins designed an experiment using 10 pairs of coral fragments. Each pair consisted of one healthy fragment and one bleached fragment originating from the same coral animal.
Five pairs were positioned so that the fragments physically touched. The other five pairs were separated by gaps measuring only a few millimeters.

The results revealed a dramatic difference. Every bleached fragment that touched its healthy counterpart recovered completely within seven weeks. In contrast, the bleached fragments that were kept apart died.
How a Simple Touch Triggers Rapid Coral Recovery
The researchers discovered that the remarkable recovery depends on a special ability of genetically identical corals to connect their tissues.

"Genetically identical corals recognize one another when they come into contact," said Palumbi, who is a professor of oceans in the Doerr School of Sustainability and of biology in the School of Humanities and Sciences. "Their tissues fuse if they are from the same clone. We see something similar in humans. Organ transplants are often successful if the donor is your identical twin."

Using a powerful microscope, Collins and his colleagues examined what happened when the coral fragments touched. They found that tiny channels within their tissues quickly lined up, forming connections that allowed materials to move between the two fragments.

Through these connections, beneficial algae and the nutrients they produce could pass from the healthy coral into the bleached one. Within just three days, researchers observed algae transferring into the damaged fragments.

The team then investigated how long the corals actually needed to remain connected. By separating pairs after different periods of contact, they discovered that a single week was enough to transfer the algae required for complete recovery. In some cases, just five days of contact produced the same result.
Remarkably, the separated corals still returned to full health within seven weeks, the same amount of time required by corals that remained connected throughout the experiment.

This finding revealed that the rapid recovery was not primarily driven by a continuing supply of algae from the healthy coral. Instead, once enough algae entered the bleached fragment, they reproduced rapidly inside their new host and restored its energy supply.
"Once beneficial algae enter bleached corals, they don't just spread out," said Palumbi. "They flood in and start dividing at the fastest rates seen in corals."

During the second week of contact, the beneficial algae living inside the bleached fragments doubled in number approximately every four days. That growth rate was about ten times faster than what researchers have observed in wild corals.
A Promising Breakthrough for Coral Reef Restoration
Scientists have spent decades searching for ways to protect coral reefs from rising ocean temperatures, disease, increasingly acidic seawater, and other environmental pressures.

Their efforts have included selectively breeding corals that can withstand higher temperatures, raising young corals in nurseries to rebuild damaged reefs, and transferring communities of microorganisms between corals to improve their resilience.
The new findings suggest another possibility: helping bleached corals recover quickly enough to survive the dangerous period following a marine heat wave.

"Bleached corals are often considered a lost cause because recovery after a heatwave is very slow, if it happens at all," said Fiorenza Micheli, the David and Lucile Packard Professor in Marine Science and a faculty advisor of Collins. "We hope this new research will inspire solutions that keep corals healthy long enough to enable full recovery after heat waves through slower processes such as growth, reproduction, and recruitment of new colonies."

However, the researchers emphasize that their experimental approach cannot yet be used to restore reefs on a large scale. For the technique to work as demonstrated, every bleached coral would need access to a healthy, genetically identical counterpart. Finding and supplying those matches across entire reefs would be impractical.
Important questions also remain about how the recovery mechanism could be adapted for broader use.
Over the coming months, the team intends to investigate other ways to introduce beneficial algae into bleached corals without requiring them to remain physically connected to healthy fragments.

One possibility involves collecting beneficial algae from healthy corals well before marine heat waves occur. Researchers could then deliver large quantities of these algae to damaged corals after bleaching events, potentially allowing them to recover much faster.

"These new insights into how corals can naturally recover give us hope for the future," said Micheli, who also co-directs the Stanford Center for Ocean Solutions. "They open the door to what's possible and may lead to the breakthrough we need to accelerate reef restoration."

Micheli also serves as a professor of oceans and (by courtesy) of biology. Both Micheli and Palumbi are senior fellows at the Woods Institute for the Environment, which is part of the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability.
Additional Stanford researchers who contributed to the study include Jana Sipkova, Nathaniel Mollica, Tom Rolander, Courtney Klepac, Gabriel Calistro, and Vanessa Barone.

Mollica is a research scientist in Stanford's Oceans Department, where Calistro works as a research assistant. Rolander is a research engineer in the Fabrication Lab at the Harold A. Miller Library at Hopkins Marine Station, which belongs to the Doerr School of Sustainability.

Sipkova is a postdoctoral scholar, while Klepac is a research scientist. Barone is an assistant professor in the Biology Department of Stanford's School of Humanities and Sciences and is affiliated with Bio-X and the Maternal & Child Health Research Institute.
The Molecular and Cellular Biodiversity Imaging Center, operated by Stanford's Biology Department at Hopkins Marine Station, conducted the coral image analyses.

A population of once-rare hybrid crabs has surged to record numbers, following a marine heatwave that hit the Bering Sea in 2018.
This dramatic increase in hybrid crabs is not something marine scientists had factored into their plans for managing this decimated fishery, but now they've worked out the likely cause.
Their results are published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Almost every year since 1982, researchers at NOAA's Alaska Fisheries Science Center have trawled the bottom of the eastern Bering Sea to check the state of the ecosystem.
NOAA is especially interested in keeping track of the commercially valuable species – worth hundreds of millions of US dollars each year – that call this sea home.
When a marine heatwave rolled across the Bering Sea in 2018-2019, it set off one of the most significant marine mass mortality events on record.
The effects of marine heat waves are far-reaching and often unpredictable, since we haven't historically seen these climate events unfold with the intensity they've reached in recent decades.
These marine heat waves are a direct result of the climate crisis, as we continue to burn fossil fuels, which release greenhouse gases into our atmosphere.
The ocean absorbs most of the heat trapped by these gases, which is why we're seeing marine heat waves more frequently, in ecosystems that are unprepared for such dramatic changes to the temperature.

The NOAA researchers watched the snow crab (Chionoecetes opilio) population collapse via their trawler samples. In 2018, before the heatwave, they estimated the population was about 8 billion crabs strong.
In the years that followed, those numbers began to plummet.
Then, in 2020, the researchers missed the annual trawl for the first time since it began.
When they returned in 2021, they estimated only about 1 billion snow crabs remained.
The heat wave drastically reduced winter sea ice and raised temperatures in the cold pool on the bottom of the Bering Sea, setting off a chain reaction that meant many snow crabs starved to death.
In a critical moment for the fishery, the Alaska Department of Fish and Game banned commercial fishing of snow crabs for the first time.
The ban lasted roughly two years, from 2022 to 2024.
But in the meantime, scientists noticed something very strange. They were pulling up nets with an unusual number of hybrid crabs: part snow crab, part Tanner crab (Chionoecetes bairdi).
Hybrid snow-Tanner crabs are not unheard of, but they've always been considered rare. They happen when a snow crab and a Tanner crab mate.
In 2025, the abundance of these hybrids was 13.4 times greater than the historical average.
Hybrids typically never exceeded 10 percent of the commercial-sized male crab population. In 2025, nearly half of the snow crabs available to catch were hybrids.

"Because snow-Tanner hybrid crab have historically been rare in the Bering Sea and very little is known about processes that influence their abundance and persistence, scientists and fishery managers hadn't expected hybrids to also benefit from these warmer waters," NOAA fisheries biologist Erin Fedewa told ScienceAlert.
Fedewa and team re-created the possible sequence of events via computer modeling to see which factors could have led to the sudden surge of hybrid crabs.

"Our study provides evidence that decreased sea ice during the marine heatwave drove the snow crab population collapse, which subsequently triggered increases in hybrid crab abundance, likely through reduced competition and predation from snow crab," NOAA fisheries biologist Erin Fedewa told ScienceAlert.

When two different species interbreed like this, their offspring are sometimes unable to reproduce. For that reason, hybrids are not considered a species in themselves. This kind of interbreeding could therefore further diminish the snow crab population.

"Very little is [known] about the reproductive potential of snow-Tanner hybrid crab, so it's unclear if hybrids are able to reproduce and become ecologically independent from parent species," Fedewa said.

"Because the dramatic increase in hybrids has unfolded in the past few years, the potential ecological implications of the event remain to be seen. The ecological role of hybrids remains an important research question and it's unclear what the consequences, if any, may be on parent species."
In the meantime, there are immediate consequences for fisheries management.
Legal-sized male hybrids are technically harvested as snow crab, but because they've been historically rare, they've been left out of crab harvest quotas.
That could add further problems when it comes to helping the snow crab population recover.
"It is within the purview of the Alaska Department of Fish and Game… to increase snow crab total allowable catch accordingly to reflect abundance increases in harvestable hybrids," Fedewa explained.
"However, this strategy is generally not ideal, as it poses the risk of increasing exploitation on snow crab, a population that is still rebuilding following the collapse."
The research has been published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
A cheeky-looking starfish stole the show during a live-streamed deep-sea expedition off the coast of Argentina last year, but that was not all scientists found.

An international team of biologists recently met at Universidad Maimónides in Buenos Aires to identify a trove of species collected during the Schmidt Ocean Institute expedition in August 2025, where a Patrick Star lookalike was famously live-streamed.
Within just two weeks, participants at the taxonomy workshop named 57 new species and 5 new genera that were collected with the help of the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) SuBastian.
Most of the specimens were collected from the Mar del Plata Canyon, one of Argentina's largest deep-sea rifts.
At its deepest point, Mar del Plata Canyon plunges to more than 3,500 meters below the ocean's surface.
It's also where the warm, salty Brazil current collides with the cold, nutrient-rich Malvinas current, making this one of the most energetic regions in Earth's oceans.

The expedition aboard Schmidt Ocean Institute's Falkor (too) research vessel was part of the Ocean Census's race to document deep-sea marine life across the world, before it is potentially disrupted by threats like climate change and deep-sea mining.

"The Mar del Plata Canyon expedition captured the public's imagination when we first live-streamed Argentina's deep-sea, discovering potential new marine species," says oceanographer Jyotika Virmani, director of the Schmidt Ocean Institute.
"These results show the power when world-class technology and expertise meets international scientific collaboration."

Altogether, the team identified 22 new echinoderm species (sea cucumbers and crinoids), 20 new species of copepods (a group of crustaceans), 14 cnidarians, including octocorals, sea pens, and stony corals, and one mollusc: a tusk shell.
Some of the corals, sea cucumbers, and crustaceans also represent new genera (which, in taxonomy, is the next level up from species; e.g., the Homo in Homo sapiens).

An impressive deep-sea holothurian – nicknamed 'Loki' for its horn-like appendages that resemble the Norse god's hat – was one of up to 10 new sea cucumbers discovered. It's been added to the genus Peniagone.
This vivid purple sea cucumber is a newcomer to the genus Benthothuria.
Here's one of the new sea pen species. Sea pens are strange filter-feeding animals. They look a lot like plants, but each sea pen is actually a coral colony, made up of multiple polyps.
This octocoral, with its branching structures, looks a bit more familiar, though it too is an entirely new species.

Some of the new species were much smaller, like this copepod, which is a type of crustacean. Every single copepod the biologists examined during the taxonomy sprint was new to science, contributing 20 new species and one new genus to the total.
From these tiny bug-like critters to the elaborate Loki sea cucumber, these discoveries are a reminder of just how much more we have to learn about life on Earth.
"The deep sea holds some of the least understood ecosystems on Earth," says Michelle Taylor, head of science for Ocean Census.
"By identifying new species, these scientists have advanced our understanding of South Atlantic marine life and, via Ocean Census, ensured that this data is accessible globally," Virmani adds.

A new artificial intelligence model can predict a cancer patient’s risk of dying from a single photograph of their face, according to new research. While not perfectly accurate, the model found that people with higher risk-of-death scores, in general, had a higher risk of dying.
The AI builds on how human doctors evaluate their patients’ health, says Ray Mak, a radiation oncologist at Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute, who conducted the research with his colleagues.

“We’re trained in medical school to walk into a room, look at the patient and make an assessment—an impression of how healthy, frail or sick they are,” Mak says. That decision can help determine what treatment a patient receives—surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, and more. The problem, Mak says, is “that’s really a subjective assessment.”

The AI, Mak and his team hope, could help doctors and patients make more informed, objective decisions about cancer treatment and end-of-life care.

Mak and his colleagues trained an algorithm to analyze and “learn” 40 million images of faces without giving it a specific task. They then tweaked the model to analyze new photographs in two distinct ways: first, to estimate a person’s biological age and, second, to predict cancer patients’ odds of survival.

The outcome was surprisingly accurate. In a test group of 3,820 cancer patients, more than half of those with the highest risk score—64 out of 122—died within just 90 days of when their photograph was taken. In a separate test group that included more than 38,000 cancer patients, those that looked older than their chronological age also had a higher risk of dying.

“To our knowledge, this is the first report of an AI algorithm that can directly predict cancer patient survival from a simple face photograph,” the researchers write in the study, which was published on Monday in the journal Lancet Digital Health.

The question is: How does the AI do this? For both age and death risk predictions, Mak and his team tracked where the algorithm was “looking” in its analysis, a technique they call “attention mapping.” For age prediction, they found that the AI tended to base its predictions on facial areas such as the nasolabial folds—the crease between your nose and mouth—and parts of the forehead. For risk of death, the AI tended to focus on the bridge of the nose and areas below the eyes. It’s unclear why those areas specifically correlated with a person’s risk of death.
The two analyses work better together. “When we put both the face age and face survival scores into a clinical prognostic model, we do better at survival prediction than either one alone,” Mak says.

In some cases, the AI may have been picking up on known health risks, such as smoking and alcohol use. When it came to the age estimate, smokers, for instance, were more likely to look older than their age, Mak says. The same was true of heavy alcohol drinkers.

It also didn’t matter if a photograph showed a person frowning or smiling, with or without makeup or in various lighting. For age prediction, the AI was able to account for common forms of plastic surgery, Mak says. A major exception was rhinoplasty—the AI tended to rate people who’d had a nose job as slightly older in images taken after the surgery compared with images taken before it.

Mak’s hope is that, eventually, an AI model like this could be deployed in hospitals and serve as an extra data point in doctors’ decision-making. It could also help serve as an early-warning system of disease if a patient appears to be aging faster than expected. Mass General Brigham has a patent pending for face health algorithms.

Right now the AI is not ready for the clinic. For one, the cancer survival model was trained on a Boston-area cancer patient population that was majority white. Mak and his colleagues are working to expand their training sets to include a wider diversity of faces. (To that end, if you feel comfortable doing so, you can help train the algorithm and receive a “face age” estimate by sharing your own photographs here.)
But the possibility of AI having any role in determining a patient’s treatment plan raises clear ethical questions.

Matthew Liao, a professor and director of the Center for Bioethics at New York University, who was not involved in the new research, says that the paper was “interesting” and that this kind of tool could be useful for identifying people who might be sick and in need of extra care. But he notes it’s possible that an AI algorithm could slip up—and misidentify patients as being healthy or not. “If it gets it wrong, we might be sort of not providing care to someone who actually needs it,” he says.

Liao also raised the question of insurance companies turning to this sort of technology to grant or deny coverage or employers using it to hire a given job candidate deemed to be “healthier” than another. “We really need to think through the societal implications of this thing as we try as we develop it further,” he says.
Mak, for his part, is optimistic. “There’s still a lot of development ahead and clinical testing,” he says. “But we’re really excited that that we’re launching a completely new field in medicine.”
Japan’s mission to collect samples from a Martian moon is off to a good start.

Launched atop an H3 rocket from Tanegashima Space Center just after 3:40 P.M. EDT on Monday, the Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) mission is a collaboration between the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), NASA, the French space agency CNES and the European Space Agency (ESA).

If successful, MMX will be the first spacecraft to enter orbit around Phobos, one of Mars’s two moons. The goal is to learn more about how the mysterious, small moon first formed. One theory posits that Phobos and its companion, Deimos, are former asteroids that were captured by Mars’s gravity, while another is that they are composed of debris from an ancient, massive collision with the Red Planet.
The mission could also provide clues into how organic matter, or even life itself, forms on planets.

To figure this out, MMX will spend a year flying through space, and it is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in September 2027. Once there, it will observe the Martian moon from orbit to look for two suitable landing and sampling sites, one on each side of the natural satellite. Once those sites are found, the main spacecraft will release a rover, called Idefix, onto Phobos’s surface.

The rover will first sample material from Phobos’s subsurface in its onboard lab. Later the main spacecraft will land on Phobos sometime in 2030 and gather material in its return module. That module will lift off from Mars and come back to Earth with at least 10 grams of material sometime in 2031.

“Bringing samples to our most sophisticated labs here on Earth is a multiplier for discoveries, because our most precise instruments are too large, complex or sensitive to send to space,” said ESA’s MMX project scientist Elliot Sefton-Nash in a statement. “Even after the mission has been completed, future generations of scientists will study the Phobos samples with even more advanced instruments—samples brought to Earth are the gift that keeps on giving.”
A Russian satellite came dangerously close to a Finnish-American satellite this weekend in a provocative maneuver that could foreshadow the new norm for space warfare.

According to public orbital tracking data, KOSMOS-2612, a Russian satellite launched in April with very few details disclosed, approached too close for comfort to ICEYE-X36, an imaging satellite from the Finnish company ICEYE that is owned by its U.S. subsidiary and has been used by the Ukrainian military. Nobody knows quite what KOSMOS-2612 did or what its intentions were, but the two satellites were, at most, a few hundred meters apart, with some estimates putting the distance at within 30 meters. Though the exact distance is unclear, the encounter still appears to be the closest known deliberate and uninvited interaction between two active spacecraft in low-Earth orbit.

No explanatory or corroborating statements have emerged from Russian or U.S. defense officials or from ICEYE, leaving outside experts to speculate about the apparent orbital game of cat and mouse that unfolded overhead.

Such a maneuver is not inherently aggressive or ill-intentioned, says Victoria Samson, head of space policy at the Secure World Foundation. But when taken in the context, the close approach is concerning.

“You’re looking at what Russia is doing here, not in terms, specifically, of what’s happening in space but as part of a larger examination of what’s happening on Earth,” Samson says. “Russia and Ukraine are literally at war with each other. And so it’s kind of tinting how you view Russia’s activities here.”

This maneuver is known as a rendezvous and proximity operation (RPO), and it’s not quite as straightforward as the simple formation flying that is routinely performed with airplanes. To get close to another object in orbit, a spacecraft needs to get itself into the same orbital plane and then change its velocity until it essentially matches the speed as its target so that the two don’t just zoom by each other.

Besides raising the odds of a catastrophic collision, such maneuvers usually require burning a lot of propellant, which is a nonrenewable resource. So satellite operators tend to only attempt them for very compelling reasons. In this case, the reason seems obvious: Russian officials have been unhappy about Ukraine’s purported use of ICEYE-X36’s synthetic aperture radar imaging, which can see through clouds and smoke to track and guide activity on the ground below. A Ukrainian official confirmed to Axios that the nation’s military works with the Finnish satellite company, and ICEYE announced earlier this year that it had signed a collaborative agreement with Ukraine’s defense ministry. ICEYE-X36 launched in 2024, two years after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

KOSMOS-2612’s stalking could be chiefly a warning meant to signal capability, or it could instead be intended for more direct and nefarious action: During an RPO, an aggressor satellite can do any number of things to its target, including taking pictures, jamming communications, blocking sensors or even physically disabling and pushing the other spacecraft out of orbit. Under pressure, the operators of ICEYE-X36 could well decide the spacecraft must burn precious propellant of its own to escape or elude KOSMOS-2612 or other threatening satellites, shortening the mission’s operational lifetime.

Russia’s maneuver has also come as Ukraine has faced broader interference with space-based support for its defense against Russia’s ongoing invasion: Ukrainian war fighters and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky have reported widespread throttling of SpaceX’s satellite-based Starlink and Starshield services on the battlefield.

The technology to accomplish RPOs is rapidly improving: China, the U.S., Russia and several private companies have all been independently testing their RPO capabilities for the past several years. Radar tracking data show that, since May, other KOSMOS satellites have been maneuvering around ICEYE-X36 in provocative maneuvers that have been explicitly called out by the U.S. Space Force.

There are few official international regulations related to these types of maneuvers, and conducting one nonconsensually breaks norms and crosses ill-defined lines for mutual safe operations on-orbit, Samson says. Unsolicited RPOs might be interpreted as aggressive—or even as an act of war. And already high tensions on the high frontier now seem set to soar: last month the U.S. Space Force announced that it had placed weapons in space. (The U.S. did not disclose many other details about the weapons, but some experts believe they’re communication jammers with RPO capabilities.)

Although ground-based surveillance now allows close tracking of most satellites, without public statements from operators of secretive spacecraft, it’s harder to know what, exactly, they’re up to when conducting maneuvers such as this one. Samson says there’s little to do, for now, besides watching the mysterious drama play out overhead.
“We’re going to wait and see what happens,” she says. “This kind of thing can change quickly, but I would hold off hysterical speculation until we know more about it.”

Shares of several Singapore-listed agricultural companies fell Tuesday after Senior Minister K Shanmugam warned they won't "escape responsibility" for their possible role in the haze blanketing the city-state.
"Companies cannot play hide and seek" with different corporate structures, hoping that will help them, Shanmugam said, revealing that seven companies had been questioned by the Singapore Exchange.
Bumitama Agri fell as much as 6.5%, while First Resources dropped to a low of 4.83%. Golden Agri Resources and Wilmar International slipped almost 2%.

Shanmugam, who is also home affairs minister for the city-state, said that some of the fires or smoke source points seem to be associated with First Resources, Bumitama Agri, as well as non-listed First Borneo Plantations.

"Take, for example, First Resources. It issued a detailed statement on its zero burning policy and firefighting efforts ... but statements, no matter how well drafted, are not good enough. Show us the evidence."
The other companies named by the minister were Golden Agri-Resources, Wilmar International, Kencana Agri, Indofood Agri and TSH Resources.
The haze has affected businesses and daily life in Singapore and Malaysia in the past few weeks, with the air quality in Singapore hitting levels not seen since 2015.
Schools in the state of Johor Bahru in Malaysia have also closed due to the air quality reaching unhealthy levels.

"They should not underestimate the Singapore government's determination to act," Shanmugam said, adding, "we will use every legal and regulatory lever at our disposal to exert pressure where it matters, including on their bottom lines, including on their access to financing, and including on their standing with investors."

He also revealed that Singapore could even amend laws or introduce new laws "on an urgent basis" to ensure cooperation, if needed. Companies potentially linked to the haze would also be examined if they still meet the standards for government grants or incentives.

When asked if Singapore's actions will affect bilateral relations between the city-state and Jakarta, Shanmugam dismissed the concern, saying, "Our people are suffering. What do these experts think we are supposed to do? Shiver in our shoes before we take any action to protect our own people? That's not the Singapore approach."

He was responding to a question about an article published by local media outlet CNA, which cited legal experts saying that actions taken by Singapore against haze-causing firms in Indonesia may carry diplomatic implications.

"If we think like that, there will be no Singapore, and we do not think there should be any bilateral issues. The Indonesian public is suffering as well, and it is in Indonesia's interests as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems."
He said that Singapore's actions against companies are aligned with the broad policies of Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.

Bank Indonesia faces mounting pressure to raise interest rates on Wednesday as economists revise their forecasts after global index provider MSCI warned it may downgrade the country's stock market from emerging-market status, setting off a selloff in stocks and the rupiah.

Citibank now expects a pre-emptive 50 basis-point increase to 6.25%, abandoning its earlier call for no change. Capital Economics and Permata Bank expect a 25 basis-point hike to 6%. The central bank has held its benchmark seven-day reverse repurchase rate at 5.75% since June.

MSCI said Friday it is considering moving Indonesia to "standalone" from the emerging-market status it has held since 1989, causing the Jakarta Composite Index to suffer the worst two-day sell-off recorded, before recovering about 3% Tuesday after authorities announced steps to improve market transparency and price discovery, including expelling tightly held companies from the flagship index.
Meanwhile, rupiah weakened to 18,030 per dollar on Tuesday, near its June record low, falling about 8% this year.

"Not delivering a rate hike [on Wednesday] would run the risk of disappointing investors and fueling further downward pressure on the currency," said Jason Tuvey, deputy chief emerging markets economist at Capital Economics. "A decision to hold rates on Wednesday could also revive concerns among investors that Bank Indonesia is kowtowing to political pressure."

Citi's Helmi Arman said a hike would aim to stop equity outflows spilling into bonds and prompting capital flight by domestic investors. He expects it to be a "one-off" followed by other support such as government foreign-currency borrowing or another round of bilateral currency swaps with foreign central banks.

The central bank has already raised rates by a combined 100 basis points since May. Headline inflation quickened to a three-month high of 3.28% in September, within the 1.5%-3.5% target range, while core inflation eased to 2.84%. The governor, Destry Damayanti, has said foreign-exchange reserves of $146.3 billion at the end of September would be adequate to stabilize the rupiah.

"Market confidence can deteriorate much faster than economic fundamentals," said Josua Pardede, chief economist at PT Bank Permata, estimating that foreign investors have net sold about $5 billion of Indonesian stocks this year. The risk is that foreign equity withdrawals could further weaken the rupiah and trigger selling in government bonds, he added.

An MSCI downgrade could force $3 billion to $5 billion of passive outflows, with another $15 billion of actively managed foreign money exposed to reassessment, he estimates. Pardede expects the market adjustment may come in stages, from precautionary selling through the first half of 2027 and mechanical selling if MSCI confirms the move by June.

"BI can provide liquidity and reduce excessive volatility, but only credible market-governance reforms can address MSCI's fundamental concerns," he said, calling for credible free-float data, ownership disclosure and transparent engagement with international institutional investors.
"The biggest risk is not simply losing Emerging Market status, but letting doubts about market integrity become a lasting increase in Indonesia's cost of capital."

Ann Hornaday, the longtime film critic at The Washington Post and author, died Sunday. She was 66.
Hornaday died at her home in North Baltimore after a battle with glioblastoma, a form of brain cancer, her husband Dennis Greenia told the Baltimore Banner.
A much-loved and respected film critic, Hornaday was named a Pulitzer Prize finalist for criticism in 2008.

Born March 9, 1960, in Iowa City, Iowa, Hornaday grew up in Des Moines. She graduated from Smith College in 1982 with a degree in government and later moved to New York. She freelanced for Premiere, Us and worked at the feminist publication Ms. Magazine, and became co-founder Gloria Steinem’s administrative assistant.

After taking a journalism fellowship in Athens, Georgia, where she met her husband, Hornaday would go on to work at various newspapers, including the Austin American-Statesman and The Baltimore Sun, before joining The Washington Post in 2002, replacing previous critic Rita Kempley.

At the Post she became a national figure in film criticism writing hundreds of reviews, and was known for her accessible reviews that were free of pretension. During her run as a prominent critic, she also appeared on WYPR’s Midday at the Movies program. She left the Post in 2025 after taking a buyout.

In 2017, she wrote the book Talking Pictures: How to Watch Movies, a practical guide for movie lovers on how to appreciate cinema and improve film literacy. Hornaday had also completed a book about the production of Alan J. Pakula’s classic 1976 political thriller All the President’s Men. That book is set to be published posthumously in 2028.
Hornaday is survived by her husband Dennis, daughters Victoria and Leila, and brother William.
Mariah Carey on Monday won a long-running $20 million lawsuit alleging she defamed her brother in her bestselling memoir The Meaning of Mariah Carey when a New York state court dismissed the suit.

Morgan Carey, brother to the iconic singer, first filed his lawsuit on May 28, 2021, claiming Mariah damaged his reputation in the 2020 memoir by portraying him as violent and accusing him of trafficking cocaine. In the ruling issued Monday, reported by Billboard and Rolling Stone, Justice Leslie A. Stroth of the New York State Supreme Court found that Morgan Carey failed to establish that his sister acted with actual malice.

“Plaintiff has not sufficiently pleaded actual malice on the part of [Mariah],” Justice Stroth wrote, according to the reported ruling. “Plaintiff fails to provide any proof that [Mariah] made such statements with knowledge of their falsity or with reckless disregard of their falsity or with reckless disregard for the truth. While plaintiff alleges that [Mariah] demonstrates ill will towards her brother, such statement is insufficient, and plaintiff has not satisfied the pleading requirement for actual malice.”

John Rosenberg, Mariah’s lawyer, told Rolling Stone in a statement that Mariah is “gratified that the court recognized that her memoir addresses significant issues of public interest and dismissed her brother’s defamation claims in their entirety.”

Morgan’s lawyer Richard Altman, however, told the outlet in a statement that they intend to appeal: “We respectfully disagree with today’s decision as being completely inconsistent with prior rulings in the case.”

Anyone who was introduced to Darren Criss through his role on Glee was in for a special treat Sunday night (Oct. 18) at London’s Royal Albert Hall, where the Emmy- and Tony-winning actor reunited with co-star Chris Colfer to perform together for the first time in more than a decade.

Criss joined Glee during season 2 in 2010 to play Blaine Anderson, the lead singer of the Dalton Academy Warblers and love interest (and eventual first boyfriend) for Colfer’s Kurt Hummel. On Sunday, when Criss made his debut at the iconic venue with two back-to-back performances, Colfer was among an impressive lineup of surprise guests who hit the stage.

But before Colfer arrived, Criss teased the crowd by attempting to sing one of Kurt and Blaine’s most memorable duets all by himself: “Baby, It’s Cold Outside,” from the season 2 episode “A Very Glee Christmas,” which peaked at No. 57 on the Billboard Hot 100 back in 2010. “I’m gonna do my best to sing both parts,” he told the audience, launching into the impossible solo duet. A few lines in, though, the crowd started cheering when they saw Colfer emerge.

“Hey, Darren!” Colfer casually said, to which Criss responded: “It’s been awhile!” In fact, the pair hadn’t performed together in more than a decade, given Glee wrapped its seven-season run back in 2015.
“Do you know the words to this?” Criss prompted Colfer, who assured him: “I do.”

In addition to the Colfer surprise, other surprise guests included Alan Cumming for ABBA’s “Does Your Mother Know”; Stranger Things star Gaten Matarazzo for “Lost Boys Life,” an original song Criss wrote and recorded with his late brother, Chuck Criss, for their band Computer Games; Sarah Hyland for “Suddenly Seymour” from Little Shop of Horrors; as well as her Modern Family co-star Jesse Tyler Ferguson for Adele’s “Someone Like You.”

Even before Criss was on Glee, he made a name for himself as a University of Michigan student by co-creating A Very Potter Musical, a Harry Potter-themed musical that went viral online. On Sunday night, he performed “Goin’ Back to Hogwarts” from the show joined by an ensemble of acclaimed stage performers, including Glee’s Alex Newell (Shucked, Once on This Island), Jak Malone (Operation Mincemeat), Natasha Hodgson (Operation Mincemeat) and Andrew Barth Feldman (Dear Evan Hansen, Little Shop of Horrors).

He returned to the Glee world one last time for Sunday’s shows by performing with a local youth choir for Keane’s “Somewhere Only We Know” and Katy Perry’s “Teenage Dream,” two songs he famously covered on the Fox musical comedy, as the grand finale.
Since his time on Glee, Criss has gone on to win an Emmy and Golden Globe for his role in The Assassination of Gianni Versace: American Crime Story as well as a Tony for Maybe Happy Ending.

REPUBLIC rules the top 10 of the Billboard 200 albums chart (dated Oct. 24) as, for a third time, the label is home to eight of the top 10 titles. Since Luminate’s electronically monitored music data began powering the list on May 25, 1991, REPUBLIC is the only label to have held at least eight of the top 10 titles. The company did it for the first time on the Jan. 13, 2024-dated list, and then again one week later.

In the top 10 of the latest Billboard 200, REPUBLIC — and its group of labels — has the following albums: Taylor Swift’s The Life of a Showgirl (on Republic Records) at No. 1, Morgan Wallen’s I’m the Problem (released via Big Loud/Mercury) at No. 3, Noah Kahan’s The Great Divide (Mercury) at No. 5, Drake’s HABIBTI (OVO Sound/Republic Records) at No. 6, Olivia Dean’s The Art of Loving (Polydor/Island) at No. 7, Kahan’s Stick Season (Mercury) at No. 8, Greta Van Fleet’s Palace for the People (Lava/Republic Records) at No. 9 and Drake’s ICEMAN (OVO Sound/Republic Records) at No. 10.
The only non-Republic albums in the top 10 are Olivia Rodrigo’s you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love (Geffen) at No. 2 and Ella Langley’s Dandelion (Columbia) at No. 4.

The Billboard 200 chart ranks the most popular albums of the week in the U.S. based on multi-metric consumption as measured in equivalent album units, compiled by Luminate. Units comprise album sales, track equivalent albums (TEA) and streaming equivalent albums (SEA). Each unit equals one album sale, or 10 individual tracks sold from an album, or 2,500 ad-supported or 1,000 paid/subscription on-demand official audio and video streams generated by songs from an album. The new Oct. 24, 2026-dated chart will be posted in full on Billboard‘s website on Oct. 20.

Concurrent with REPUBLIC’s achievement, its parent company Universal Music Group can once again lay claim to nine of the top 10 titles. UMG is the only entity — since Luminate’s data began powering the chart in 1991 — to hold at least nine titles in the top 10. In addition to all of the REPUBLIC albums, UMG is also home to the No. 2 title, Olivia Rodrigo’s you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love (Geffen/Interscope Capitol). UMG last had nine of the top 10 on the Nov. 29, 2025-dated list.

Oct. 19 (UPI) -- More than a dozen U.S. lawmakers announced Monday that suspicious envelopes had been sent to their offices, joining dozens of colleagues already targeted by similar mailings, many containing white powder, just weeks before November's midterm elections.
The letters, first reported Tuesday, have been sent to lawmakers from both political parities across the nation.

Lawmakers who announced Monday that suspicious letters had been sent to their offices included Reps. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va.; Joe Neguse, D-Colo.; Jason Crow, D-Colo.; Brittany Pettersen, D-Colo.; Diana DeGette, D-Colo.; Chellie Pingree, D-Maine; Debbie Wasserman Schultz, D-Fla.; Becca Balint, D-Vt.; Greg Stanton, D-Ariz.; Adam Smith, D-Wash.; Adam Smith, D-Wash.; Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz.; and Adelita Grijalva, D-Ariz.
Senators who announced Monday that letters had been sent to their offices included John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., and Ron Johnson, R-Wis.
Some of the suspicious envelopes did arrive at the lawmakers' offices while others were intercepted by postal investigators.

"I can confirm that my office in Leesburg received an envelope containing a suspicious substance," Subramanyam wrote on social media Monday afternoon. "The office was promptly evacuated. Thank you to the Leesburg Police, Loudoun County Fire and Rescue and their Hazmat team and the Capitol Police for their swift response.
"These acts of political intimidation have no place in our country," he wrote.

Johnson said the suspicious envelope was delivered to his Milwaukee office at 2:38 p.m. CT Monday. He said the return address matched the description of letters sent to the offices of other lawmakers, though he did not make public what the address was.
"My staff immediately isolated the envelope, cleared all staff members and called 911 and the Sergeant at Arms," he said on social media.
"The first responders confiscated the letter, and thankfully, everyone is safe. Our office operations have now resumed as normal."
Both Pingree and Wasserman Schultz published pictures online of the suspicious letters their offices received, showing that the addresses were handwritten.
"Such cowardly acts of coercion will not work and have absolutely no place in our politics," Wasserman Schultz said in a statement.
"And to be clear, they will not deter me from fully representing my Broward County constituents."

While the return address of the letter Wasserman Schultz posted online was redacted, the letter posted by Pingree was not and bears a New York City address formerly used by the Democratic Socialists of America.
DSA spokesperson Priscilla Yeverino has previously said in a statement that the group is not involved in the letters in any way.
"We are glad to learn no one was harmed," she said.

Other lawmakers who have reported such incidents include Reps. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., and Eugene Vindman, D-Va., and Sens. Adam Schiff, D-Calif.; Pete Ricketts, R-Neb.; Ted Cruz, R-Texas; and Mike Rounds, R-S.D., among others of both major parties.
Schiff said Sunday that at least one envelope containing a suspicious substance was sent to his offices in California and was intercepted by U.S. Capitol Police and the Senate Sergeant at Arms.

"This attempt to intimidate elected officials and our staff will not succeed," Schiff said. "We instead condemn these threats as antithetical to the values of our nation, recommit to our work and thank the law enforcement and postal officials who are helping keep our teams safe."

The incidents apparently started Tuesday, when Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry and the Oklahoma State Election Board reported receiving envelopes with a similar white powder. The Senate Sergeant at Arms, Capitol Police, FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating.

Oct. 19 (UPI) -- The Department of Homeland Security said Monday that more than 100,000 Ukrainians and Sudanese in the United States would remain shielded from deportation for the time being under a humanitarian immigration program that the Trump administration has sought to curtail.

Both Ukraine and Sudan have been designated for Temporary Protected Status, a program that prevents eligible nationals already in the United States from being deported to their home countries that are experiencing life-threatening conditions due to war or natural disasters.

The previous Biden administration extended TPS protections for El Salvador, Sudan, Ukraine and Venezuela for 18 months during its final days before leaving office to the Trump administration, which has announced terminations of TPS designations for 13 countries, including Venezuela, though litigation has blocked some terminations from taking effect.
TPS for Sudan and Ukraine was to expire Monday.
DHS did not state it was extending TPS for either country, but that "an announcement" concerning their statuses "will be made at the appropriate time."
Until the announcement is made, Ukrainians and Sudanese present in the United States under TPS will "retain protection including work authorization."
There are about 103,700 Ukrainians and 1,900 Sudanese TPS beneficiaries, according to government estimates.

Ending TPS, arguing the protection was only supposed to be temporary, has been among tactics of the Trump administration's execution of its hardline immigration crackdown, raising the prospects of deportation for immigrants, some of whom have lived in the United States for decades under the TPS program.
"We're grateful for an extensions, however temporary, for TPS holders from Ukraine and Sudan," Myal Greene, president and CEO of World Relief, said in a statement Monday.

The Christian humanitarian organization has been among those calling on Congress to pass legislation creating long-term legal protections for those who cannot return to the war-ravaged countries such as Ukraine and Sudan, rather than creating an atmosphere of uncertainty for those who wait to learn whether their TPS status will be renewed.

"TPS is intended to be temporary, but unfortunately, conflict and instability don't respect our preferred timelines," Matthew Soerens, vice president of advocacy and policy at World Relief, said in the statement.
"We're grateful that Ukrainian and Sudanese TPS holders can go a bit longer without fear of having to return to war zones, but that relief is fleeting."

Daniel Delgado, former deputy assistant secretary for immigration policy at DHS under the Biden administration and current senior policy fellow at the Washington, D.C.-based Searchlight Institute, criticized the Trump administration on Monday for leaving the Sudanese and Ukrainian TPS-protected individuals in limbo by not making a decision on their status.

"Instead of clear guidance to help inform the life-altering decisions that thousands of Ukrainians and Sudanese will be forced to make, DHS and this administration would rather they live with an increasing sense of uncertainty and anxiety," Delgado said in a statement on social media.
"There's a process in place to determine whether a country warrants TPS. It is a choice to not follow it."
The Biden administration initially designated Ukraine for TPS following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Sudan has had TPS status since 1997, though the first Trump administration unsuccessfully sought to terminate its designation. The Biden administration then issued a new designation for Sudan in March 2022 amid a political and humanitarian crisis in the African nation following an October 2021 military coup that preceded the outbreak of the country's ongoing civil war in April 2023.
Oct. 19 (UPI) -- Authorities in parts of France have imposed curfews Monday as the country recovered from widespread protests over the weekend that turned violent in places.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu asked some cities to establish "partial curfews" in response to the events, in which at least two people killed and more than 2,000 were arrested.

The curfews include one from 11 p.m. Monday to 6 a.m. Tuesday local time in Paris' Place de la République and another from 10 p.m. Monday to 6 a.m. in the streets around Les Halle, CNN reported. There are other curfews in Lyon, Marseille, Nice and other cities and communities.

The protests started in September with high students demonstrating for better school and education conditions. The protests spread to university students, union leaders and others concerned about the cost of living, remaining mostly peaceful.

Over the weekend, however, things turned more violent in places. Some rioters took to vandalism, setting buildings on fire, breaking windows and looting from shops. These incidents took place in major cities across the country, including Paris, Limoges, Bourdeaux, Grenoble, Nice, Marseille, Lyon, Rennes and Strasbourg.
French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday asked for calm, saying that the "legitimate demands" of students had been hijacked by looters and those causing destruction.
"I've asked the government to provide all the lessons learned and to be able to anticipate it to make sure that this does not happen again," he said. "We need unity, we need calm and respect."
Earlier Monday, Macron rejected French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez's offer to resign after the protests.

A statement from the Élysée Palace, the office of the presidency, said Macron refused Nuñez's offer "given the need for continuous command of the security forces in the current situation." Macron, instead, asked Nuñez to employ "new methods of action on the ground as quickly as possible ... against violent rioters," EuroNews reported.
Macron said he planned to hold meetings this week to address protestors' concerns and demands.

Lecornu said the government will set aside money to help affected areas recover from the damage and that there will be a partial unemployment fund for those unable to work due to the riots and looting.
The head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry said more than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been affected and that damages were at hundreds of millions of euros.
In the United States, meanwhile, President Donald Trump and J.D. Vance blamed the riots on immigration.
"The migrants have taken over France," Trump wrote in a social media post Monday morning. "They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!"
Over the weekend, meanwhile, Vance said he hoped that Americans were paying attention to the violence in France and claimed that "this is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country."
