Since it first opened its doors on Bastille Day in 1883, the city hall of Limoges, France, has been celebrated as an architectural wonder. Well known for its tall spire and ornate metal belfry, the 143-year-old building gained historic monument status in 1975 as a prime example of late 19th-century French architecture and civic pride.

On the building’s parapet, the city’s coat of arms was framed by mosaic portraits of four famous former residents, who lived in Limoges between the 16th and 19th centuries: Leonard Limosin, an enamel painter; Henri François d’Aguesseau, a jurist who served as a chancellor of France; Pierre Victurnien Vergniaud, an orator and figure of the French Revolution; and Jean-Baptiste, Count Jourdan, a military commander and one of Napoleon’s marshals.

But this weekend, much of the city hall was destroyed in a blaze that French authorities immediately characterized as arson. Amid antigovernment protests that have gripped France in recent days, masked individuals forced their way into the building on Saturday evening and set fires that spread to cause extensive damage, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP).

“Today, the entire facade and the historic front section have been almost 100 percent destroyed,” Maurice Barate, a top regional official, said on national television, per the New York Times’ Giulia Imbert. The spire and roof also collapsed. Barate called the arson a “catastrophe for heritage” and a “deliberate act by hooligans,” according to AFP.

The physical extent and emotional toll of the town hall’s damage was immediately compared to that of Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris, which burned extensively in 2019, likely as the result of an accident, not deliberate arson. Over 12 hours, the inferno destroyed most of the 12th-century cathedral’s roof, spire and exterior decorations, though many religious relics and artworks inside were salvaged.

The Notre-Dame tragedy struck an emotional chord not only in France but around the world. Donors raised close to $1 billion to support the cathedral’s reconstruction. In 2023, a new spire was raised, and in late 2024, it officially reopened to the public.
“It broke my heart. I saw Notre-Dame all over again, except this time it was our town,” Francoise Faurie, a Limoges resident who witnessed the fire, tells Reuters’ Clotaire Achi.

Leaders are calling for monetary support from the French government. “I want us to have the same capacity to rebuild as was given to Notre-Dame de Paris,” Guillaume Guérin, the mayor of Limoges, told local media, per the Telegraph’s Vivian Song. “I want to see a rain of millions on the city.”

In the blaze’s aftermath, fire crews and other emergency personnel continue to monitor the building for possible signs of collapse and other infrastructural weaknesses. Standing further back, residents have come to pay their respects to the building, which was a popular location for events such as baptisms and wedding ceremonies.

“All we have left are pictures,” Gilles Peignelin, who married his wife in the building, told the New York Times as he stood beside her and looked at the ruins. “I’m outraged—it’s shameful, deplorable.”

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) is sending a spacecraft toward Mars to help solve an enduring mystery of the solar system: Where did the Red Planet’s two lunar companions, Phobos and Deimos, come from?

JAXA’s Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe launched from the agency’s Tanegashima Space Center in southern Japan on October 20 at 4:41 a.m. local time (October 19 at 3:41 p.m. Eastern time). If all goes according to plan, the Japan-led mission will bring samples from Phobos, the larger of the lunar duo, back to Earth in five years. These precious bits of dirt could finally reveal how the moon and its smaller sibling came to be, while also shedding light on Mars’ history.

“Despite their potential importance, Martian moons have never been fully investigated,” JAXA planetary scientist and MMX project manager Yasuhiro Kawakatsu tells the Associated Press’ Mari Yamaguchi. “They are known as the most important unclimbed mountains in the solar system.”

There are two main hypotheses about Phobos and Deimos’ creation. One posits they may have formed the same way Earth’s own moon formed: Something slammed into Mars and shot tons of material into space, which eventually coalesced into the two moons. (Why this would have birthed dual mini moons, rather than a single large one like Earth’s, remains an open question.) The other possible explanation suggests that the two bodies were asteroids sucked into Mars’ orbit millions of years ago, according to a statement from NASA, which is contributing to MMX. Other collaborators include the European Space Agency, France’s National Center for Space Studies, the German Aerospace Center and the Australian Space Agency.

Both scenarios carry significance for understanding their host planet. If Phobos formed from Martian debris, it could be made of material from Mars’ earlier days, when the Red Planet may have been better predisposed to host life than it is now, according to a JAXA statement. On the other hand, if Phobos hails from the far reaches of the solar system, it may have brought along water-bearing minerals and organics that could’ve helped birth life on Earth.

Scientists are hoping that the MMX mission, which is slated to reach Mars’ system in August of next year, will help solve the matter. The spacecraft will first investigate Phobos from orbit before landing on the moon’s surface twice in separate locations to collect the highly anticipated samples. The MMX probe will also investigate Mars from a distance and perform flyby observations of Deimos.

“We’re going to choose a first landing site and then do some landing operations, and after that we’re going to lift off and get back to orbit,” Tomohiro Usui, a JAXA planetary scientist and member of the MMX team, tells CNN’s Ashley Strickland. “It takes another several months for the search of the next landing site. Landing operations are very risky.”

The mission will collect samples on Phobos via two instruments. One will collect ground surface samples by acting like a vacuum cleaner. It’ll emit bursts of high-pressure nitrogen gas to loosen the dirt and suck up the disturbed regolith. The other sampler will pull cores from a few inches deeper in the ground. Only 0.35 ounces of material will be transported back to Earth, but that’s plenty for scientists to work with, Chrysa Avdellidou, a planetary scientist at the University of Leicester in England who is working on the mission, tells BBC News’ Rebecca Morelle, Alison Francis and Kevin Church.
“We can do several studies even on individual grains. … You don’t need to have kilos back from a surface in order to do science. So, it’s worth every gram,” she tells the outlet.

If MMX is successful, it would become the first mission to return a sample from a Martian moon, and it could be the first to complete a round trip from the Martian system. And because scientists suspect Phobos has gotten sprayed with debris from asteroid impacts on Mars, the returned samples could include bits of the Red Planet. Phobos was chosen as the landing destination mainly because it’s the moon closest to the host planet, and therefore more likely to have Martian dust, reports the AP.

Only 1 percent of the material collected might be from Mars, Kiyoshi Kuramoto, a planetary scientist at Hokkaido University in Japan and MMX team member, tells Science’s Robin George Andrews. Still, that tiny fraction of otherworldly dirt might carry evidence of extraterrestrial life. “I do think there’s a possibility that chemical traces of biological activity might be contained within that sand sample,” Kuramoto says.
Archaeologists in Scotland have unearthed the remains of a controversial structure near Glasgow that was the nexus of a violent 1823 clash over land rights and private property.

In the early 19th century, a wealthy Scottish distiller named Thomas Harvie bought an estate in the countryside just east of Glasgow. Taking issue with a public pathway along the River Clyde that cut through his property, Harvie built two 12-foot-tall, heavily fortified walls on either side of his estate, blocking the public from using the path. The walls became known as Harvie’s Dyke, a Scottish term for a stone wall.

“The people of Glasgow [were] quite up in arms against this,” Edward Stewart, an archaeologist with Archaeology Scotland, tells the Scotsman in a video. In 1823, a mob of discontented locals from the East End of Glasgow marched to Harvie’s Dyke and destroyed the walls with gunpowder and explosives that coalminers brought from the mines.

A militia dispersed the mob and arrested participants. Harvie rebuilt his walls, topping them with iron spikes, broken glass and small cannons. But the Glaswegians fought back again, this time through a lawsuit that reached as far as the House of Lords. In 1828, the Lords ruled in favor of the people of Glasgow, and Harvie was forced to install gates in the dike to establish the public right of way through his property.

This year, archaeologists and volunteers took part in “Digging the Dyke”—a collaborative excavation organized by the Glasgow Building Preservation Trust, Glasgow City Council, Glasgow Life and Archaeology Scotland—at a location along the River Clyde where historical records suggest Harvie’s eastern wall once stood.

The excavation unearthed what researchers believe are foundations of the demolished wall, as well as a rare 1791 token engraved with the phrase “Let Glasgow Flourish,” per a statement. Opponents of the dike in the 1820s adopted that slogan as a rallying cry, suggesting that the coin may have been purposefully dropped near the site. Researchers also discovered pieces of mortar, slate and plasterwork that may have composed one of the dike’s defensive structures.

As Glaswegians rallied against Harvie’s Dyke, Harvie became a “pariah figure,” per the statement. The public boycotted his whiskey, and Harvie frittered away his fortune on legal bills. “Harvie never really recovers from this,” Stewart tells the Scotsman. “All because of his hubris and his unwillingness to allow people to take access through his land.”
Meanwhile, the people of Glasgow rejoiced. Their 1828 victory against Harvie inspired poems, songs and commemorative medals.

“The Harvie’s Dyke protesters had developed a green consciousness long before the Green Party was established,” Christopher Whatley, an emeritus historian at the University of Dundee and author of Harvie's Dyke: The People, Their Liberty and the Clyde, tells the Herald’s Jody Harrison.
Later, the campaign against Harvie’s Dyke was evoked throughout the 19th century to prevent landowners from blocking long-used walkways, Whatley said in a 2025 lecture.

“Let the people remember the famous battles of Harvie’s Dyke and take courage,” wrote the Glasgow Weekly Herald in 1884. “That the banks of the Clyde should be free … is in cause a matter of life and death to our humbler citizens, who are in growing danger of suffocation from want of pure air in the city and free spaces in the country.”

Archaeologists have unearthed an 11th-century wooden kitchen gadget with an ancient board game carved into the back. Medieval bakers may have used the wooden paddle not just to transfer bread into an oven but also to pass the time while they waited for the food to cook, the researchers said.

"We discovered a fragment of a fairly large shovel," Sergey Toropov, director of Novgorod State University's Center for Archaeological Research, said in a translated statement. "Most likely, it was a bread shovel, which was used to bake bread in an oven. On the reverse side, however, three squares have been carved, one inside the other."

The "bread shovel" — also known to contemporary home bakers as a wooden bread peel, a pizza paddle or a pizza peel — was found at the archaeological site of Pyatnitsky in the center of Staraya Russa, a medieval town between Moscow and St. Petersburg where last month, archaeologists reported their discovery of a "snake amulet."

The preserved portion of the bread peel measures about 12 by 16 inches (30 by 40 centimeters), and it was likely crafted from oak. While one side is flat, likely for baking tasty treats, the other side had been carved with a board for the ancient game known as merels, merrelles, mills, nine-men's morris or cowboy checkers.

The origin of the game is unknown, but historical records and archaeological artifacts suggest a similar two-person logic game was played by the ancient Romans two millennia ago — and the game may be even older than that. In the Middle Ages, merels became particularly popular across Europe and Asia, possibly because it requires little equipment and can be set up quickly.

A typical merels board has three nested squares connected by horizontal and vertical lines. Each player has nine pieces of the same color. The goal is to arrange the pieces into columns of three along the lines. When a player forms a line, they can remove any one of their opponent's pieces. In this way, merels is a mixture of tic-tac-toe and checkers. A player wins when their opponent has only two pieces left or is completely blocked. (You can play an online version here.)
"Perhaps special boards for playing merels existed in antiquity," Toropov said, "but more often, one finds playing boards scratched or carved into the flat surfaces of household objects."
The archaeologists are not sure whether the wooden bread peel served two functions or whether it was repurposed as a game board after it broke and was no longer useful.
"At any moment, one could mark out a board on a flat surface, find suitable pieces — for example, small stones lying underfoot, and while away some time," Toropov said.

Merel boards and playing pieces have been recovered from ninth-century archaeological sites in the kingdom of the Rus', whose ancestors were Vikings who arrived in what is now Russia in the eighth century, according to the statement, but "a find as well-preserved as the one from Staraya Russa is practically unique."

A gene variant called APOE4 dramatically increases the risk of late-onset Alzheimer's disease, the most common form of dementia. Now, emerging research is revealing APOE4's true role in the condition, and a new study pinpoints a possible way to treat it.

Historically, scientists studying Alzheimer's disease have focused on two proteins that accumulate in patients' brains: amyloid-beta and tau. However, there's a "third thing that people didn't pay attention to, until recently," said study co-author Li-Huei Tsai, a neuroscientist at MIT. That third thing is the accumulation of droplets of fat, or lipids, in the brain, she told Live Science.

The APOE gene makes proteins responsible for transporting fat around cells throughout the body and brain. A version of the gene called APOE4, which increases the risk of late-onset Alzheimer's three- to 12-fold, makes proteins that are less efficient at this function, Tsai said. But how APOE4 affects different brain cells was not clearly understood.
Tsai's team has been working to close that gap for about a decade.
"APOE4 can influence many different cell types," she emphasized. "It's not just one cell type."

In past laboratory research, Tsai's team found that APOE4 causes a buildup of cholesterol in astrocytes, star-shaped brain cells that support the function of neurons. Genetic analyses suggested that the gene variant may mess with how these cells process fat.

Another study zoomed in on oligodendrocytes, cells that help insulate neurons' outgoing wires with a fatty material called myelin. This material helps neurons send messages more efficiently. APOE4 caused the oligodendrocytes to accumulate cholesterol. So, in lab mice, the team used a drug to help the cells get rid of that extra cholesterol, and it improved the cells' ability to make myelin and the mice's performance on cognitive tests.

In their latest research, published Thursday (Oct. 15) in the journal Cell Stem Cell, Tsai's team dug into the question of why APOE4 causes fat to accumulate in the first place.

They used stem cells to grow APOE4-carrying oligodendrocytes and then turned specific genes on or off, to see if they increased or decreased the formation of fat droplets. This screening pointed to a major group of genes involved in cell-to-cell communication, called the Wnt signaling pathway. This included a key gene called DKK1, which acts as a brake on this signaling system.
Disabling DKK1 — essentially lifting the brake — reduced the concentration of fat droplets in the cells, the team found.

In brain tissue samples from organ donors with APOE4, the team also found signs of low Wnt signaling. This finding "establishes a very strong link" between the signaling pathway and formation of fat droplets, said Rosie Jackson, a cell biologist at the University of Dundee who was not involved in this study.
The researchers then investigated exactly how Wnt signaling was disrupted in oligodendrocytes.

APOE4 seemed to decrease the cells' supply of a protein that helps relay Wnt signals. That helpful protein was being broken down by an enzyme whose levels had been boosted by the APOE4. In mice, the team used a drug to block that extra enzyme, and the treatment ultimately restored normal Wnt signaling, reduced fat buildup, and helped the cells make myelin properly.

This could change how scientists think about treating Alzheimer's disease, Jackson said. It "opens up a new wave of potential therapeutics" that could target the accumulated fats, rather than going after only amyloid-beta and tau, she said.

"I think that this is becoming a really common idea in the field — that we're going to need multiple medications that target slightly different elements," she told Live Science. "And targeting lipids will be a really important part of that."
That said, the findings have not been confirmed in humans yet.

"It's very encouraging that facilitating lipid clearance and lipid movement is a potential therapeutic avenue," said study co-author Joel Blanchard, a neuroscientist at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. The question is how we can do that in a safe and effective manner in humans, he said.

Blanchard has led other research that underscores APOE4's effects beyond fats and myelin. The gene variant may affect cells that support blood vessels in the brain by driving scarring and contributing to amyloid-beta buildup. It may also mess with the "trash collectors" inside astrocytes, again leading to a buildup of harmful proteins.
While cells with other versions of the APOE gene can put a lot of energy toward breaking down the proteins, APOE4-carrying cells put all their energy toward fat storage, Blanchard said.

But more research is needed to understand how to fix the problem, he said. Hopefully, targeting fat storage "could rescue not just one thing but multiple things that go wrong in the course of Alzheimer's disease," he told Live Science.

What it is: A copper plate with a hammered decoration
Where it is from: Cahokia Mounds, Illinois

This copper plate was discovered in the late 19th century in a prehistoric Native American burial at the Etowah Indian Mounds archaeological site in Georgia, but it was likely made hundreds of miles away at Cahokia Mounds in Illinois. While the decorative plate showcases long-distance trade and a shared ritual culture among early Indigenous groups in the southeastern United States, the nature of the human figure depicted on the artifact has been debated for over a century.

The "Birdman" relic is one of two hammered copper plates that Smithsonian archaeologist John P. Rogan unearthed in the 1880s while digging in a burial mound at Etowah, a centuries-old village occupied by thousands of Native Americans from 1000 to 1550. Etowah was part of the "mound-building," or Mississippian, phase of Indigenous occupation; other famous sites include Moundville in Alabama and Cahokia in Illinois. These groups had extensive trade networks and shared a common artistic and ceremonial tradition known as the Southeastern Ceremonial Complex.

This copper artifact, known as Rogan Plate 1 or the "Birdman" plate, is in the collection of the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C. The plate is roughly 11 inches (28 centimeters) tall and had been buried with a high-status person who likely died at Etowah in the mid-14th century. But experts believe the copper plate was an heirloom made decades earlier, at Cahokia, and traded south to Etowah.

A human figure dominates the copper plate with its elaborate bird costume. The person carries a severed head by the hair in their left hand, while their right hand holds a club or mace. The figure also wears a pleated skirt or loincloth that may have been made from human scalps. This bird-human figure is commonly depicted in the Southeastern Ceremonial Complex and has been called a dancing warrior, eagle warrior, eagle dancer, hawk dancer, falcon dancer and falcon warrior. But more often, the figure is called Birdman or Morning Star, a prehistoric Mississippian hero associated with agriculture and rebirth.

Archaeologists' interpretations of the Birdman plaque from Etowah have long assumed that the represented figure is a male warrior. In a 2004 study, for example, archaeologist Adam King wrote that "this plaque would have served as an emblem of office awarded to a chieftain, and would have accompanied him as a sign of his strength among the ancestral spirits."

But the sex of the skeleton in the Etowah burial is unclear, and there were high-status graves of both men and women at Etowah, archaeologist Billie Follensbee and art historian Katie Buford wrote in a 2017 study. Although experts previously assumed that both Rogan Plate 1 and Rogan Plate 2 represented male warriors, Follensbee and Buford found that the figures have slender bodies with prominent right breasts, suggesting the "Birdman" may have actually been female.

"A female bird-human warrior could have represented a gender variant individual in the form of the well-known Native American phenomenon of the 'manly-hearted woman,' a woman who has assumed the usually male role and the garb of a combat soldier," Follensbee and Buford wrote. In addition to the historic term "manly-hearted woman," third-gender or gender-variant individuals in Indigenous North America are often referred to as "two-spirit," a broad term Indigenous people coined in 1990 to describe people who take on gender-nonconforming roles.

The commemoration of a two-spirit individual on a copper artifact, as well as the use of the artifact as a high-status grave good, "not only demonstrates the Native American cultural acceptance of such gender variant roles but also further serves to celebrate the elite status and achievements of these 'manly-hearted women,'" Follensbee and Buford wrote.

Running a successful parts store requires more than knowing which part fits which vehicle. It takes effective inventory management, dependable delivery service, employees who understand customers’ needs and a manager who can connect everyday decisions to the store’s financial performance.

NAPA is giving independent store owners new resources to develop those capabilities through NAPA Academy, extending training developed for its company-owned stores to independent businesses. The program was introduced during the 2026 NAPA Store Owner and Field Sales Meeting, held Sept. 21-24 in Atlanta. The initial offering focuses on store managers, combining short online courses with a downloadable resource guide designed to help translate training into daily practice.

Introducing the program, Cassie Bell, NAPA’s senior vice president of HR, said the expansion supports the company’s Drive 2030 strategy and its investment in people. Although owners have requested training for several positions, she said store managers were a logical starting point.

“We believe fundamentally that the store manager is critical to obtaining consistent customer service, to building the teams and driving those operational performances inside of our stores,” Bell said.
The program’s development began with a practical question: What do successful employees and stores do differently?

Jesse Parrish, NAPA’s director of learning and development, said the Academy worked with teams across the organization to identify the knowledge, skills and behaviors that define excellence in specific roles. NAPA partnered with industry professionals to turn those findings into training, reference materials and learning pathways.

By observing high-performing managers and market directors in top-performing stores, the team identified the practices and strategies driving their success. Those real-world insights became the foundation for new training programs designed to help others apply proven strategies throughout the organization.

For store operations, the resulting framework has four areas of emphasis: driving financial results, leading and developing teams, enabling operational excellence and delivering exceptional customer service.

Those areas address responsibilities ranging from understanding store performance and building improvement plans to coaching employees, managing inventory, optimizing delivery service and building customer loyalty.
The team documented those practices in how-to guides, training courses and tools intended to help other stores apply them.
The online courses generally take 10 to 20 minutes to complete. Owners can take the courses themselves or assign them to employees, allowing training to address specific development needs.

Although the first offering centers on store management, its usefulness extends to other positions. Parrish pointed to customer service lessons, including effective phone conversations, as examples of content relevant to counter employees.
“It is not just limited to the store manager,” he said. “While the content’s focused on them, there are relevant courses here for others that may be frontline workers working the counter.”

That connection matters because a store’s customer experience depends on both management decisions and individual employee interactions. Training managers to coach their teams complements instruction that helps counter professionals better serve wholesale and retail customers.

The second major resource is a downloadable store manager guide. It outlines the role’s responsibilities, key functions and performance metrics, with linked how-to guidance covering subjects such as budgeting, performance management, customer service and root cause analysis.
Parrish described its purpose in everyday terms: helping employees understand “how do you do the work on a Tuesday morning at nine o’clock?”

The training framework recognizes three proficiency levels: foundation, advanced and mastery. Foundation focuses on performing a job independently and effectively. Advanced emphasizes consistently meeting performance targets and helping others succeed. Mastery involves anticipating opportunities, leading broader improvements and consistently exceeding targets.
That structure provides a development path for employees with different experience levels, from someone entering a management role to an established leader seeking to improve store performance.

Participation is voluntary, Parrish emphasized, with independent owners able to use the resources as they see fit within their businesses. The materials are intended to remain within the NAPA family. NAPA also is exploring how to tailor resources further to independent owners’ needs.

Bell encouraged owners to access the content, develop a plan for using it and return regularly as materials are updated. She also asked them to share feedback about missing resources or opportunities for improvement.

“If you need something more, you need something different, something’s not working, whatever that looks like, please reach back out to us,” Bell said. “We are only as good as the feedback we’re receiving from you.”

The fifth-generation Ram 2500 places substantial demands on its brakes. Many of these trucks carry heavy payloads, tow trailers or operate in fleets, so a successful brake job requires a complete-system inspection and parts that match the platform’s thermal and mechanical demands.

This Brake Job covers the 2019-present fifth-generation Ram 2500, not the Ram 1500. The 2500 uses heavy-duty components and platform-specific procedures. Confirm the model year, engine, axle and options before ordering parts or applying specifications.
The Ram 2500 has four-wheel vented discs and dual-piston sliding calipers. Separate parking-brake shoes act against a drum surface inside each rear rotor hat.

Booster configuration depends on the engine. The 6.4L Hemi uses a dual-diaphragm vacuum booster and an electric vacuum pump near the left front of the engine to supplement engine vacuum. The PCM commands the pump based on operating inputs. The 6.7L diesel uses Hydro-Boost, supplied by the power-steering pump, with an accumulator providing limited reserve assist if pump pressure is lost.

When it’s practical, begin the process with a road test and note pedal travel, assist, pull, vibration and noise under normal braking. Confirm the complaint before disassembly; a vibration blamed on the front brakes may originate at the rear, and an assist complaint may come from the vacuum or power-steering circuit rather than the foundation brakes.

Clean around the master-cylinder cap and verify that the fluid is at the MAX mark. On a diesel vehicle, you should also inspect the power-steering fluid level, hoses and lines, because Hydro-Boost depends on that circuit. Low fluid, leaks, restrictions or weak pump output can create assist complaints. On gasoline models, inspect booster vacuum plumbing and electric-pump operation.

Compare inner and outer pad wear and both sides of each axle. Uneven wear can reveal seized hardware, binding pads, piston trouble or slide problems. Replace pads as an axle set if usable lining at the thinnest point is 1 mm (0.04 inch) or less. Inspect boots, pistons, slides, hoses and bleeders for damage, leakage and corrosion.

Be sure to measure the rotors. Minimum thickness is 37.4 mm (1.47 inches) front and 32.4 mm (1.28 inches) rear. Maximum runout is 0.020 mm (0.0008 inch); maximum loose-rotor thickness variation is 0.008 mm (0.00031 inch). You should also inspect the internal parking-brake surface; maximum drum diameter is 207.2 mm (8.157 inches).

Support the caliper and adapter; never let the hose carry their weight. Clean the pad lands and hub face without removing base metal. Install new anti-rattle clips, verify free pad movement and make sure both pistons retract smoothly. Because the rotor fits over the hub studs, hub cleanliness and uniform wheel-fastener torque are critical to controlling installed runout.

Rear service adds the parking-brake assembly. A rotor that will not release may be hanging on the shoes, so release the pedal and back off the star wheel if necessary. With the rotor off, inspect the shoes, springs, adjuster, cable action and drum surface. Clean the hub and bracket, verify piston and slide movement, and install new hardware and sealing washers as required.
Always replace caliper hardware; old clips can restrict pad movement and cause uneven wear.

Use fresh fluid meeting SAE J1703-F and DOT 3 standards. Bleed in this order: right rear, left rear, right front and left front, keeping the reservoir full. For pressure bleeding, use the correct adapter; 15-20 PSI is generally sufficient, depending on equipment limits.

If air entered the HCU, perform a base bleed, use a capable scan tool’s ABS Miscellaneous menu to run the HCU bleed routine, then bleed the base system again. Set the fluid level and verify a firm pedal.

Hydro-Boost is generally self- bleeding. Fill the power-steering reservoir, disable the engine and crank it for several seconds, then recheck the level. Re-enable and start the engine, slowly turn lock to lock twice, shut it off and discharge the accumulator with five pedal applications. Restart, repeat two slow lock-to-lock cycles, shut down and correct the level. If the fluid foams, let it dissipate before repeating the final cycles.

Adjust the shoes before cable tension. With the pedal fully released and the front cable slackened at the frame-rail adjuster, turn each star wheel through the backing-plate hole until slight drag is felt, then back it off until drag disappears. Adjust both sides equally.

Cable-tensioner adjustment is normally required only after replacement or disconnection. After verifying cable movement and shoe adjustment, fully apply the pedal. Mark the non-threaded tensioner rod 1/4 inch from the tensioner edge and tighten the nut until the mark disappears. Release the pedal, confirm both wheels rotate freely, verify that the brake holds and road-test the truck.

Ever drive a vehicle that just doesn’t feel right anymore? Maybe it wanders down the highway. Maybe there’s a clunk every time you hit a pothole. Maybe the steering wheel isn’t centered, the tires are wearing unevenly, or it just doesn’t inspire the confidence it used to.

The truth is, steering and suspension problems rarely come from a single worn out part. Every control arm, ball joint, tie rod, sway bar link, and bushing work together as one connected system. When one connection starts to wear, it puts added stress on the rest of the system, and before long, that small problem becomes several bigger ones.
That system level approach is exactly how TrakMotive has positioned its Suspensia brand chassis program. Learn more about it in this video, sponsored by TrakMotive.

Buchholz said it also evaluates adjacent categories for “low friction” opportunities where it can create value quickly. In many cases, some of MotoRad’s strongest product ideas have originated with technicians, counter professionals and other customers who identify ways the company can improve a product or make a repair easier.

Looking ahead, Buchholz said MotoRad’s growth strategy centers on three areas: commercial execution, operational agility and technology. Commercially, the company plans to continue listening to the market, responding faster and creating greater value through areas such as coverage, service, business intelligence and quality. Technology supports both priorities by improving efficiency, reducing waste and helping the company respond to rapidly increasing expectations for speed.

Circle track racing represents one of the most technically demanding environments for an internal combustion engine. Whether the surface is dirt or asphalt, these engines must survive sustained high rpm, extreme lateral g-forces and the unpredictable conditions that develop over the course of a race night. Unlike drag racing engines built for seconds of peak output, circle track powerplants must deliver broad, controllable power for hundreds of laps while maintaining durability.

That balance between power, drivability and longevity defines successful circle track engine development. According to Luke Wilson of 4 Piston Racing and Jack Cornett of Cornett Racing Engines, designing an engine for this environment requires a different mindset than nearly any other racing discipline. The two builders gave us their perspectives on engines for this application.

One of the defining characteristics of a competitive circle track engine is how usable its power is throughout the race. Conditions change constantly during an event, particularly on dirt tracks where the racing surface evolves lap after lap.

Early in the evening, dirt tracks may be heavy and fast, rewarding engines that produce strong high-rpm horsepower. But as the racing surface changes and slicks off, the characteristics required from the engine can shift dramatically.

“In qualifying and early heat races, the tracks can be heavy, so big, high-rpm power can be the fastest thing out there,” Wilson explains. “If there are yellow flags and restart after restart, a good, strong, low-end grunt engine may work you through to the front.”
Later in the night, drivers may be forced to maintain speed with minimal throttle input as traction becomes scarce.

“As the track slicks off in the longer races, the driver has to have the ability to run around the track fast at as little as 40% throttle…then be able to dig into their bank of power as they find places in the dirt that will hold more,” Wilson says.
This constantly changing environment means builders rarely chase peak dyno numbers alone. Instead, they focus on creating an engine with a broad, controllable powerband.

“The real balance is in making sure an engine is responsive on a restart, strong through the middle and can carry rpm to your mandated rpm,” Wilson says. “The engine has to be smooth and controllable by the driver, who is sitting in a strange position and bouncing all over the place.”

While power delivery is critical, durability is equally important. Circle track engines spend extended periods operating at extremely high rpm, which creates unique challenges for internal components.

“In circle track racing, the engine has to be built with endurance and longevity in mind,” Cornett says. “It’s completely opposite of drag racing or tractor pulling. Our engines must go 600 miles at 9,000 rpm.”

Sustained operation at these speeds places enormous stress on the rotating assembly and valvetrain components. Builders must carefully balance lightweight choices for acceleration with materials capable of surviving long-term fatigue.
“Selecting bottom end components is a balancing act,” Cornett explains. “You want the lightest components possible for acceleration, but they have to be durable enough to last thousands of miles.”
This philosophy extends to the entire engine package, from connecting rods and pistons to camshaft profiles and valvetrain components.

“Compromises have to be made in an endurance application with camshaft profiles and valvetrain components, compression ratio and ignition timing, plus carb jetting,” Cornett says. “All these factor heavily into the longevity of the engine.”

One of the most critical systems in a circle track engine is lubrication. Sustained lateral forces during cornering can starve engines of oil if the system is not designed specifically for oval racing.
“The oiling system in our engines has to be dry sump only,” Cornett says. “There is no way the engine can survive without it.”

Dry sump systems allow builders to maintain a stable oil supply while also managing oil control within the engine. Specialized oil pans and tanks are engineered specifically for left-turn racing and the lateral g-forces the engines and cars experience.

“Good, clean, non-aerated oil is critical to longevity,” Wilson says. “These engines typically have good dry sump systems that will work well on these short runs. Controlling where that oil goes and how clean the oil supply is gives you a longer-lasting engine.”
Because engine architectures vary widely across circle track classes, oil pressure requirements can differ significantly as well.

“There are very short-stroke engines with big pins on both ends, and there are smaller-displacement, small-bore, large-stroke engines – like what we build – that really require a different type of oil pressure and rebuild schedule,” Wilson notes.

Temperature management is another critical factor in circle track engine performance and reliability. Unlike many drag racing engines that run relatively cool, circle track engines often operate at significantly higher temperatures for extended periods.

“In dirt midget racing, engines are preheated to 190 degrees F with diesel or electric units and then they go push off and run,” Wilson explains. “They never have a problem having temperature in them. In fact, many of them are run too hot.”
Limited cooling capacity and the challenges of racing on dirt often contribute to high operating temperatures.

“They have small radiators with no fans, and they can get packed with dirt,” Wilson says. “Teams often come off the track with engines that have more temperature in them than the engine builders want to see.”
Cornett notes that maintaining proper operating temperatures is essential for engine survival.

“Heat management is very important and it becomes critical on dirt due to the surface you are racing on,” Cornett says. “We want to keep the water temp in the 200-240 degree F range and the oil temp in the 220-260 degree F range.”
Fuel tuning is sometimes used as an additional method of temperature control. “They often are running rich lambda outside of optimal to help keep the engines cool,” Wilson says.
Clearances, Bearings and Ring Strategies
While circle track engines operate in extreme conditions, many builders rely on proven fundamentals when it comes to internal clearances.
“There is no black magic here,” Wilson says. “Run your bearing clearance that you would normally run for your engine you are building and the oil you are running.”
For the engines built at 4 Piston Racing, that typically means clearances between .0018” and .0022”. However, Wilson notes that he’s seen other run larger clearances without engine issues as well.

Ring gap selection follows a similar philosophy. Run the ring gaps that your piston design engineer determined for your piston. “Adjust as you analyze your engines when they come back for service,” Wilson says.
One factor builders must monitor carefully is the presence of excess fuel in the ring lands, particularly when running methanol with constant-flow fuel systems.

“I have observed many times where teams run overly rich on these constant flow systems and will have a lot of unburned methanol sitting in the ring lands,” Wilson says. “There is power and longevity in having this properly managed.”
Cornett notes that ring gap strategies continue to evolve as piston and ring designs become thinner, narrower and more efficient.
As with most forms of motorsport, rulebooks play a major role in shaping circle track engine architecture.
“Rules dictate everything we do,” Wilson admits. “But this type of racing can often leave you a lot of flexibility in individual internal decisions.”
Builders typically maximize displacement and rpm within the limits set by sanctioning bodies, but internal design decisions still allow room for innovation.
“If you took the top five engines out there, you’d see some significant differences in how they are built because the engine architecture is so different,” Wilson says.
In some classes, that freedom is one of the reasons circle track racing remains attractive to engine builders.

“There is a lot of parity in midget engines,” Wilson says. “It is about as blank sheet as you can get for wanting to build something you can call yours. Many other types of racing have gone too far on requiring a spec engine.”

Cornett echoes that sentiment from the perspective of dirt late model racing, saying, “Rules are obviously always a big concern on how to build your engine. Luckily, in dirt late model racing, there aren’t many rules.”

Despite careful engineering, circle track engines face numerous potential failure points based on engine type as each has a different Achillies heel. According to Cornett, two issues appear more frequently than others.

“The two most common failures in circle track racing are bearing failure and overheating,” he says. “I think most bearing failures are caused by not properly warming up the oil temp before you race. Overheating issues are usually caused by racing on dirt.”
Wilson notes that valvetrain components and timing drive systems can also be vulnerable.

“Engines can see valvetrain and rod bearing issues because of how the racers beat them on the limiter repeatedly,” he says. “Crashes can create additional risks. The most common failure is in the timing drive system when a car is turned backwards, flipped, or crashed in a bad way.”
Ignition system limitations can also contribute to engine stress in some racing classes.

“We have observed repeatedly where we are asking for 25 degrees of timing and will see an engine walk around as much as 10 degrees in either direction,” Wilson explains. “This is really hard on engines and easily resolved by putting a modern motorsports grade ignition system on the engine.”

Because circle track engines operate under extreme conditions, regular service and inspection are essential for maintaining performance and reliability. Cornett Racing Engines typically bases rebuild intervals on total laps run.
“Based on our experience, we have developed a lap strategy to know when to rebuild the engine,” Cornett says. “The customer keeps up with how many laps he races.”
Most engines are serviced after roughly 1,200 to 1,500 laps, which equates to approximately 600 to 750 miles of racing.
Wilson notes that service intervals can vary widely depending on how teams operate their equipment.

“I have the same engine that I’m confident that team A can run for 25 shows and then bring it for service,” he says. “I have the same engine with team B and I have them bring it back after 10 shows, sometimes in a box and not on a stand.”
Driver behavior, maintenance practices and tuning decisions all influence how long an engine survives between rebuilds.
“Some teams beat the hell out of stuff and aren’t kind to their engines,” Wilson admits. “You have to handle each team on a case-by-case basis and then develop a plan going forward.”
The Future of Circle Track Engine Technology

Even with decades of development behind them, circle track engines continue to evolve. Wilson believes that modern electronics and fuel systems could significantly improve reliability and performance in some classes.

“Midget racing specifically needs to allow some modern electronics and fueling,” he says. “Many series still rely on constant-flow fuel injection systems, which came about in the 1940s. The reality is the guys who know it well and tune it well are aging out.”

Wilson has personally tested modern electronic fuel injection systems against traditional mechanical setups. The results demonstrated that modern systems can be competitive while offering improved tuning efficiency.

“With a highly experienced constant flow pro we spent more than six hours tuning that engine,” Wilson recalls. “I swapped the injection over to my EFI, hooked up my ECU and swung a dyno pull. It cleared what we achieved on the first pull.”
Within a handful of pulls, the EFI system produced measurable gains.
“After six dyno pulls we had a smoother power curve, more responsive power and more peak power by 8–10 horsepower on a 400-hp engine,” Wilson says.
Despite the results, many teams remain loyal to traditional systems – a reminder that racing technology often evolves as much through culture as engineering.

For engine builders, circle track racing offers a unique challenge. The engines must deliver high power, survive extreme conditions and adapt to constantly changing track surfaces – all while operating within rulebooks that vary widely from one class to another. That complexity is exactly what keeps builders engaged.
“This always changing dynamic is what makes the engines in this racing so much fun to work with,” Wilson says.

As both Wilson and Cornett emphasize, success in circle track racing ultimately comes down to balancing engineering precision with real-world durability – building engines that can not only make power, but keep making it lap after lap.

A quick-release hub nut, side-position brake, top-dead-center weight indicator, and tiered placement indicators accelerate setup and correction. Onboard storage includes a high-volume top tray, side cone pegs, and a side shelf designed to accommodate Ranger Quick-Peel adhesive tape weight rolls.

A mid-year update to CCC Intelligent Solutions’ 2026 Crash Course report on industry trends and repair data shows higher-cost claims, older vehicles driving up total losses, technology-rich newer vehicles, and consumers with less financial flexibility.
CCC’s report states that claims frequency was down 3.5% through September compared with an 8.3% decline through the same period in 2025.
Repairable estimates declined 5.4%, compared with a 10.4% decrease a year earlier. Total loss valuations increased 1.1% after declining 3.1% through September 2025.
Non-comprehensive repairable claims decreased 4.2%, compared with an 8.9% decline a year earlier. Total loss valuations increased 1.4% after declining 1.2% through September 2025.

CCC notes that the composition of changes in claim volume shifted somewhat in 2026, with collision and comprehensive claims accounting for 80% of total volume reduction, compared with about 90% in 2025.

“First-party filings continue to be influenced by increased deductibles, premium sensitivity, and consumers’ willingness to absorb smaller losses themselves,” CCC writes. “The result is a system processing fewer claims, but a mix increasingly concentrated toward losses that are less discretionary.”

The share of driveable vehicles deemed total losses reached 11.2% through the first half (H1) of 2026, up from 10.3% a year ago, and 6.3% in 2022. CCC writes that, historically, over 80% of all driveable vehicles deemed total losses are seven years old or older. Non-driveable total loss frequency also increased to 52.5% in H1 across all loss categories.
CCC says repair cost inflation flattened in H1.
The average total cost of repair (TCOR) reached $4,821 in H1, 0.6% above H1 2025.
“This is a significant deceleration from the 15.7% increase recorded in H1 2022,” CCC writes. “Since 2020, however, the average has still risen from approximately $3,331 to more than $4,800.”
CCC adds that average part prices remained 8% higher year over year through early 2026, while labor rates increased by 1.5%.

“The increases in average price per part are generally aligned with tariff activity, the landscape of which continues to evolve in 2026,” CCC writes. “Most notably, the White House has announced 50% tariffs on Canadian automobiles and auto parts under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, beginning January 1, 2027. If they are implemented like current Section 338 measures, they would apply in addition to existing duties, with no exemption for USMCA-qualifying goods.”

While repair inflation has normalized, CCC says the underlying cost base remains more than 40% above 2020 levels. According to CCC, 27% of Q1 non-comprehensive claims included more than 15 parts, and fewer than 32% exceeded 30 labor hours. And both measures were shifting toward less-intensive repair bands.
Higher insurance deductibles have also become the norm, according to CCC’s findings.
Repairable collision claims carrying deductibles of $1,000 or more reached 28.4% in H1, up from 25.7% a year ago and 20.3% in H1 2022.

“For consumers, a higher deductible can provide immediate premium relief,” CCC writes. “For the claims ecosystem, it changes the economics of filing. A $1,000 (or higher) deductible makes relatively minor damage easier to postpone, self-fund, or leave unrepaired. That removes smaller claims from the population and raises the apparent severity of those that remain, not to mention exacerbating the share of total losses.
“H1 2026 data suggests that affordability-driven coverage decisions are becoming embedded in the claims mix rather than representing a temporary response to premium increases.”

CCC notes findings from a recent VIU by Hub Insurance survey: 67% of policyholders said covering a $1,000 unexpected home or auto expense would be a struggle, with about 1 in 5 of them (21%) calling it “a serious hardship” or “significant struggle.”
CCC says the first half of the year also brought total loss frequency to another high.

Through Q2, 23.5% of claims across all loss categories were flagged as total losses, up 0.8 percentage points year over year. Non-comprehensive total loss frequency reached 24.1%. CCC says that means both results extend the climb from the 2022 lows of 18.2% and 19.4%, respectively.

“Higher total loss frequency is partly a product of loss economics, but filing behavior also affects the denominator,” CCC writes. “When lower-severity first-party claims are not reported, fewer small repairable claims remain to dilute the total loss share. The customer implications are material. CCC’s Moments of Truth study found that 40.4% of insureds with a confirmed total loss switched carriers, compared with 7.6% following a repairable claim. As personal auto competition increases, total loss handling becomes not only an operational challenge but also a retention issue.”

The mid-year update touches on the aging vehicle fleet as well, which CCC says is now visible throughout the loss mix. CCC writes that vehicles seven years or older represented 74.3% of total loss valuations in H1 2026, with vehicles between seven and 12 years old accounting for 41%, compared with 33.4% in 2020.

“An older fleet does not automatically mean a simpler claim,” CCC writes. “Older vehicles carry lower adjusted values and can cross total loss thresholds quickly, even after damage that leaves them operable. At the same time, many still contain technology that requires diagnostics or specialized procedures.”

CCC also found that self-pay repair is becoming “a meaningful parallel market,” representing 26% of repair orders in H1 2026, up 0.5 percentage points year over year. The average ticket was $1,941. By comparison, CCC says the average repairable insurance claim was $4,821 and more than 71% of self-pay orders were below $2,000, while 75% of insurance repairable claims exceeded that amount.
The report also touches on diagnostics trends in collision repair and the hybrid and electric vehicle segments.
In Q1 2026, CCC says 74.8% of repairable appraisals included a scan and 29.9% included a calibration, up from 70.9% and 23.3%, respectively, a year ago.
Among DRP appraisals, scan penetration reached 89.8% and calibration penetration reached 40.6%, according to CCC.

“More than 83% of industry scans appeared on the initial estimate, while 47% of calibrations were captured there,” CCC writes. “For DRP claims, 93.1% of scans and 50.9% of calibrations appeared on the initial estimate. This suggests diagnostics are becoming less of an exception discovered later in the repair and more of a recognized requirement at intake.”

Regarding hybrid vehicles, CCC says they represented 9.9% of repairable claims in Q2 across all vehicle ages compared with 4.3% for electric vehicles. Among vehicles three years old or newer, the hybrid share reached 19.0%, while EVs were 9.5%.

For vehicles three years old or newer, average hybrid TCOR reached $6,415 — $435 below the EV average of $6,850. Since 2020, CCC says hybrid repair costs have increased 53.6%, compared with 16.3% for EVs. EVs remain the most expensive fuel type in this age group, according to CCC.

For collision shops investing in ADAS equipment and training, access to protected vehicle systems is essential to putting that investment to work. Technicians need to communicate with the vehicle, perform the required procedures and document the results before a repair is complete.

Autel continues to expand those capabilities through software development, secure gateway access and improvements shaped by technician feedback. Across supported Stellantis, Nissan, Mercedes-Benz and Volkswagen/Audi vehicles, that work gives appropriately equipped shops more opportunities to perform diagnostics and ADAS calibrations in-house.
The benefit is practical: greater control over scheduling, fewer handoffs and more opportunities to put the shop’s equipment and technician expertise to work.

Security gateways protect vehicle systems by restricting certain diagnostic and service functions to authenticated users. For an independent shop, having a compatible diagnostic tool and calibration equipment is only part of the equation. Access to protected functions can determine whether the technician can complete the job.

Autel provides secure gateway access for supported Stellantis, Nissan and Mercedes-Benz vehicles through AutoAuth, an online service that authenticates registered shops and technicians. Supported Volkswagen and Audi SFD access is available directly through compatible Autel tablets.
Depending on the vehicle, system and tool, authenticated access enables protected operations such as clearing codes, performing Active Tests and initiating supported ADAS calibration procedures.

Shops should confirm vehicle-specific coverage and account requirements before scheduling the work. Maintaining the applicable Autel software subscription, authorization service account and internet connection helps technicians arrive prepared to access the functions they need.
Autel’s work to expand secure access spans multiple vehicle manufacturers and years of development.

In June 2020, Autel introduced AutoAuth-based gateway access for supported Fiat Chrysler Automobiles vehicles, now part of Stellantis. Nissan Central Gateway access through AutoAuth followed in May 2024. By December 2024, Volkswagen/Audi SFD access was available directly through compatible Autel tablets.

Autel announced initial Mercedes-Benz security-gateway access through AutoAuth in January 2025, followed that July by enhanced access for additional protected operations on select 2021 and newer models, including supported ADAS calibrations.

“With access to this enhanced gateway, Autel users can now perform additional services, including ADAS calibrations, on the latest Mercedes vehicles,” said Paul A. Marshall, Director of Product Development for Autel U.S., when the company announced the capability in July 2025.
Further Nissan software development has expanded supported diagnostic and calibration functions on eligible MaxiSYS tablets, adding more late-model applications to the work shops can perform.
Each expansion serves the same purpose: helping independent technicians access the vehicle functions required to complete supported repairs.
Access becomes valuable when technicians can use it successfully on the vehicles in front of them. That requires compatible equipment, clear instructions and careful preparation.

Autel’s calibration software presents vehicle-specific setup guidance to help technicians prepare the vehicle, position the equipment and follow the applicable procedure. Accurate calibration depends on meeting requirements for vehicle condition, target placement, working environment and verification.

On Autel’s optical positioning systems, software safeguards require verified setup measurements to fall within specified tolerances before technicians can proceed. These checks help identify positioning problems before calibration begins and reduce the risk of failure caused by incorrect setup.

Autel also continues to develop equipment for different shop environments and service models. The MA800 mobile calibration system, for example, combines laser-guided positioning with independent pitch, roll and yaw adjustment to help technicians establish the required target position.
Together, vehicle access, setup guidance and calibration equipment help shops turn supported coverage into completed work.
Completing a calibration also means documenting what was done.

Autel’s scan reports and calibration records help shops communicate diagnostic findings and procedure results to estimators, customers, insurers and others reviewing the repair. Keeping those records with the job supports a clearer account of the work performed.

Autel continues to refine its reporting based on feedback from collision repair shops, mobile service providers, ADAS calibration businesses and technicians. That feedback helps guide improvements to the information available to both the person performing the work and the person reviewing it.

As vehicle technology advances, shops need tools that continue to improve with it. Expanded access, broader coverage, clearer procedures and useful documentation all contribute to the value of their equipment investment.

Autel’s commitment extends across research, engineering and technician education, with a focus on helping shops perform supported work accurately and efficiently. The technicians using these tools every day remain central to that effort: their experience helps identify what needs to improve and where development can make the greatest difference in the repair bay.
For collision shops, that commitment means more opportunities to keep work with the team responsible for the repair—and greater confidence in the tools supporting it.
